documents.abstract: This study compares Claude and ChatGPT against teacher marking of handwritten Psychology examination scripts, examining how prompt design affects large language models (LLMs)–human agreement. Sixty-nine handwritten scripts, as photographic images, were graded by both LLMs under four prompting strategies (minimal, rubric, exemplar, role-based). Both LLMs differed significantly from the teacher in seven of eight conditions; Claude under role-based prompting was the sole exception (p = 0.038). ChatGPT overmarked across all four prompts, while Claude’s deviation varied across prompt conditions. Prompt type had a significant impact on grading accuracy with a significant LLM × Prompt interaction (p = 0.001, η²p = 0.08). Claude under the exemplar prompt had the closest agreement with the teacher’s marks (MAE = 2.42; r = 0.84). A grade-level analysis showed that scoring accuracy did not always result in grade-level agreement, indicating both metrics are needed. Prompt design improved LLM grading accuracy, but neither model reproduced teachers’ marks closely enough to replace human oversight in high-stakes assessment.

Green-aviation research on battery and alternative-fuel chemistries has advanced rapidly, but a persistent blind spot remains: the psychological readiness of the maintenance personnel who operate these systems daily under safety-critical conditions.Silver-zinc (Ag-Zn) batteries, used in fighter aircraft for their high energy density, evolve hydrogen and oxygen gas through electrolysis of their alkaline electrolyte during charging -a hazard that builds invisibly over 36-to-72-hour charge cycles and becomes dangerous only once hydrogen concentration crosses its lower explosion limit.Managing this hazard depends less on chemistry knowledge and more on sustained technician vigilance during a long, low-stimulation monitoring task -precisely the condition under which classic vigilancedecrement research shows attentional lapses emerge, independent of training or competence.Drawing on the author's two decades as an aviation electrical maintenance engineer and a second career in applied and clinical psychology within the same defence environment, this paper argues that emerging green-energy-storage chemistries (lithium-ion, solidstate, hydrogen fuel cells) will introduce comparable low-visibility, highconsequence hazards, and that maintenance-crew psychological readiness must be engineered alongside the chemistry itself.Integrating self-efficacy theory, the Technology Acceptance Model, and vigilance-decrement research, the paper proposes a Psychology-Chemistry Interface Model with three components -chemistry-literacy calibration, hazardtolerability screening, and stress-buffered reporting culture -and a training framework for building calibrated, sustained vigilance in ground crews adopting new energy chemistries, including a low-cost toolkit -a pre-task hazard card, a vigilance-rotation roster, a hazard-tolerability selfcheck, and an added prompt within existing incident-reporting procedures -deployable at a single maintenance unit without new infrastructure.

Background While Sino-African higher education cooperation is expanding, it is unclear whether and to what degree short-term programs (e.g., scholarships) have consistently translated into progress, such as sustainable growth at the individual, institutional, and societal levels in both China and Africa, particularly in the era of artificial intelligence (AI). Both the pandemic and AI have transformed public-health education, research, and practice while introducing unprecedented issues regarding data governance, algorithmic bias, privacy, and technological inequity. However, there is a dearth of theoretical insights on sustainable Sino-African cooperation, particularly in the context of public health talent development in the AI era. To bridge this gap, this study aims to investigate how resources and capabilities can be transformed into sustainable, reciprocal public-health talent development. Methods An integrative review was conducted following the five stages proposed by Whittemore and Knafl in 2005: problem identification, literature search, data evaluation, data analysis, and findings presentation. The Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines informed the processes of evidence identification, screening, eligibility assessment, and synthesis. Heterogeneous evidence concerning China–Africa cooperation, public-health talent development, AI and digital health, knowledge co-creation, institutionalization, and responsible AI governance was critically evaluated and synthesized across micro-, meso-, and macro-levels of Sino-African collaborations. Results A total of 11 articles met the eligibility criteria. Based on detailed analysis of the evidence, the China–Africa Transformative AI Logistics & Young Scientist Talent System (CATALYST) was developed. The framework positions young public-health talents as both the central developmental outcome and active agents of collaboration. At the micro level, equitable capability and resource co-creation support talent development; at the meso level, reciprocity, trust, and knowledge co-creation facilitate translation into education, research, policy, and practice; and at the macro level, institutional mechanisms enable sustained system-level cooperation. AI functions as both an enabling technology and a domain requiring responsible governance. Conclusion The CATALYST framework provides a theoretically grounded pathway from resource sharing to knowledge co-creation and ecosystem-building, offering a foundation for designing sustainable, reciprocal, and ethically governed China–Africa public-health talent-development initiatives and for subsequent empirical validation.

Artificial intelligence (AI) can contribute to environmental sustainability while causing environmental problems. From the perspective of adaptive governance, we ask what the governments of Japan and South Korea would have to learn from their publics at the initial stage of adaptation. Using a 2024 survey of 700 citizens in each country, we find public support for a firm-targeted subsidy and a tax, with the tax receiving more support in both countries. Support was associated with concern about climate change and AI, and with anticipated environmental effectiveness. Trust in government was associated with subsidy support in Japan; no other trust association survived sensitivity analysis. Anticipated negative economic impact was associated with stronger tax support, though on a different time horizon in each country. We argue that support reaches further toward coercive instruments than innovation-first governance assumes, and that learning from it would require institutionalized citizen inputs and information on policy effects.

Traditional bibliometric indicators often fail to capture the multidimensional nature of scientific contributions, reducing complex intellectual identities to simple numerical scores. This study introduces a structural-semantic framework designed to quantify impact and innovation by integrating collaboration patterns with research topics. We model the complete population of 1,229 Italian computer science scholars using a hybrid 896-dimensional representation space. Our methodology combines structural graph embeddings derived from co-authorship networks with semantic representations of publication abstracts, utilizing transformer-based models and density-based clustering. To enhance interpretability, we employ a two-stage pipeline using large language models to generate scientifically coherent labels for identified research themes. Our integrated approach captures academic identity, paving the way for the creation a quantitative measure of research similarity. The framework successfully distinguishes researcher roles—such as specialists and interdisciplinary connectors and identified over 100 potential collaboration opportunities between researchers with shared expertise but no prior history of working together. Longitudinal analysis revealed three distinct waves of innovation in the Italian computer science landscape over the past 40 years, shifting from foundational theoretical infrastructure to applied artificial intelligence and health informatics. Furthermore, the model showed high predictive validity in forecasting future research interests. This framework provides a robust tool for science policy and institutional planning, offering a more faithful representation of scientific evolution than traditional citation-based metrics.

In this session, four LIS instructors will discuss how we question artificial intelligence (AI) technologies—from practical to policy to critical perspectives. Panelists will address questions about systems (e.g., academic policy, ethics, long-term professional impact) and our questions to systems (e.g., crafting effective prompts, using AI for fact verification). Generative AI platforms and their rapid uptake have had immense impacts across industries and everyday life (Blick, Blandin & Deming, 2024). Their seemingly-ubiquitous and sometimes surreptitious integration into everyday tools fuels a narrative of “inevitability” (see, e.g., Cole, 2026; Noonan, 2025; Yoo, 2025). Despite concerns about academic integrity, critical thinking, and bias, many faculty feel pressure to adopt AI without strong institutional guidance or confidence in their understanding (Committee on Artificial Intelligence and Academic Professions, 2025). LIS faculty must consider professional expectations, as information professionals are increasingly expected to integrate AI and support patrons’ digital literacy. Librarians must understand technical and ethical dimensions, develop relevant competencies, and keep pace with evolving tools (Coffey, 2023; Rood, 2026). However, narratives of inevitability can foreclose important discussions about choice and agency for faculty, students, and the communities that librarians support (Appedu, 2025; Baer, 2025). If they believe that AI is inevitable, people are likely to believe they have no choice but to learn about and use these technologies, regardless of whether they want to use them, perceive them to be useful, or have any critical or ethical misgivings about them. The sense of urgency can lead to uncritical adoption of the technologies, even while acknowledging the risks and ethical issues (Committee on Artificial Intelligence and Academic Professions, 2025). Faculty may also be cajoled into adopting AI technologies from the sense that their students are already using them anyway, ignoring researching showing students often have negative attitudes towards AI and do not want to use it (Holterman, 2026; Jargon, 2026; McClain, Anderson, Sidoti & Bishop, 2026). Similarly, some librarians are pushing back against the narrative of inevitability and calling for “AI Refusal” (Fox, 2025; Slater, 2025). Given the competing tensions and expectations, how can LIS faculty best address AI in their teaching? To what extent do we have a responsibility to address AI to prepare students for the realities of the field and to what extent do students (or faculty) have agency over when and how to interact with AI tools? Panel Structure: Brief introduction (Laura Saunders, 5 minutes), short panel presentations (10 minutes) and open discussion. Mei Zhang teaches courses in collection development and management, research methods, and technologies for information professionals. Grounded in a socio-technical approach, her teaching incorporates AI-related assignments that encourage students to both question AI systems (e.g., their assumptions, data, and ethical implications) and engage with them in practice. Zhang will reflect on the design and implementation of these assignments, including varied student responses—ranging from enthusiastic adoption to resistance—and the pedagogical questions these reactions raise for the role of AI in LIS education. She will invite discussion on how instructors might navigate these tensions, including how and whether to require AI use in LIS education. Don Simmons’s research centers on AI fluency and practical strategies for integrating AI tools and initiatives across multiple fields in the LIS profession. Building on his course, AI and Its Applications in the LIS Profession-- one of the few LIS offerings that comprehensively examines artificial intelligence and generative AI across libraries, archives, and museums; along with examining the historical, ethical, and sociopolitical dimensions of AI-- Simmons will highlight the importance of AI fluency in LIS, emphasizing practical, day-to-day applications for information professionals. He will introduce effective prompting strategies to support LIS workflows, including the TAP method (Think, Ask, Play), a framework he developed. Grounded in evidence-based iterative prompting this approach has produced positive outcomes through in-class experimentation with students. Laura Saunders teaches and writes in the areas of public services, reference, library instruction and information literacy. Drawing on scholarship and a critical pedagogy/ andragogy background, she will outline some AI skills and knowledge that might be important to address in these courses, explore how traditional skills such as the reference interview and neutral questioning remain relevant, and discuss how to highlight that continuity for students. She will also explore some of the pushback to AI content and share ideas for approaching AI assignments that preserves some student agency. Sarah Appedu is a PhD candidate whose dissertation research and teaching takes an agency and ethics-oriented approach to critically interrogating AI as a sociotechnical phenomenon. While access to AI tools and skills is often prioritized in many AI literacy initiatives, Sarah empowers librarians to ask the hard questions that go beyond issues of access and consider the ways in which AI can be in conflict with the very values we’re trained to embody. Her work aims to problematize the inevitability narratives surrounding AI use that are often perpetuated by the technology industry by centering librarians’ commitments to sustainability, the public good, equity, and intellectual freedom & property. She will present sets of critical questions related to each core value of librarianship that enable both technical knowledge of AI systems and agentic responses to their possibilities, limitations, and ethical consequences. The panelists will have several questions prompts prepared to help facilitate the conversation: Do LIS faculty have a need or obligation to integrate AI into their curricula? Why or why not? Have you experienced pressure either to integrate or to avoid AI in your teaching? Are you currently addressing AI in your teaching? If so, what activities, strategies or topics have you found to be effective? If not, what are your reasons for not addressing it? What are your experiences around student use of AI? What are your thoughts on AI inevitability and AI refusal? How can we navigate these tensions? The panel will be relevant to LIS instructors addressing or considering addressing AI in their curricula.

documents.abstract: Generative AI is increasingly used to prepare feedback, explanations and learning materials in higher education, raising a practical question beyond authorship: how suitable are these texts for the learners who read them? Four linked exploratory studies examine this question through perceived reader burden, defined as immediate feelings of fatigue and effort, alongside linguistic differences, source classification and computational rewriting. In a comparison involving 110 university students, an AI-generated news passage received a higher mean score than a human-written passage on an exploratory six-item reading-burden composite (3.20 vs. 2.05). To understand how these passages differed linguistically, the news pair was analysed alongside matched academic and blog pairs. Across all three, AI-generated passages showed higher lexical diversity, whereas readability and sentence-length variation followed less consistent patterns. The investigation then examined computational methods: logistic regression and an RBF-SVM achieved high accuracy in classifying text sources within their evaluation settings, whereas the RoBERTa-based detector achieved lower accuracy. Rewriting reduced heuristic scores but did not consistently produce coherent prose. Finally, an independent analysis of 60 cybersecurity passages found mixed linguistic patterns and limited success in recovering individual passages’ intended registers. Together, these findings suggest that reader burden, linguistic characteristics and source classification offer distinct forms of evidence rather than interchangeable indicators of educational suitability.

Wearable electronics have garnered considerable interest owing to their transformative potential in motion and health monitoring, artificial intelligence, human–machine interaction, and the Internet of Things. At the heart of these systems lie flexible sensors, including strain, pressure, temperature, and electrophysiological devices, that serve as essential building blocks for wearable platforms. Among the diverse materials explored for such applications, carbonaceous materials, comprising carbon fibers, carbon nanotubes, graphene, and their derivatives, stand out as particularly attractive candidates by virtue of their superior electrical conductivity, mechanical robustness, biocompatibility, and process compatibility with flexible substrates. Consequently, substantial research efforts have been directed toward the controlled synthesis and structural engineering of carbon materials to meet the stringent demands of next-generation electronics. This review provides an overview of recent progress in carbon-based flexible sensors, with emphasis on their classification and practical utility. Following a concise introduction to relevant carbon materials, the fundamental operating principles of typical flexible sensors, namely strain, pressure, temperature, and electrophysiological sensors, are examined. Subsequently, their prominent applications in motion monitoring, human–machine interaction, and healthcare monitoring are critically discussed. The review concludes with an assessment of current challenges and future directions, aimed at guiding continued innovation in carbon-based flexible sensors for advanced wearable electronic systems.

Digital transformation in Islamic higher education has driven fundamental changes in academic data management systems, particularly regarding the role of PDDIKTI operators in Private Islamic Higher Education Institutions (PTKIS). The shift toward technology-based administrative systems demands improvements in digital literacy, work motivation, and organizational readiness to support accurate, efficient, and sustainable data management. This study aims to reconstruct the work motivation of PDDIKTI operators through a needs-and-expectations approach in the digital era, while identifying the psychological, technological, and organizational factors influencing operator performance. This study employs a literature review method analyzing 20 scientific articles published between 2022 and 2026, utilizing literature collection, selection, thematic grouping, and qualitative descriptive synthesis stages. The results indicate that digital transformation through academic information systems, e-learning, Dapodik, and the utilization of artificial intelligence (AI) enhances work efficiency, service quality, and data accuracy. However, challenges persist, including low digital literacy, high administrative workloads, technological adaptation needs, and suboptimal organizational support. This study contributes to the development of a conceptual model that integrates motivational, technological, and managerial aspects as a foundation for understanding the work motivation of PDDIKTI operators in the era of digital transformation at PTKIS. The limitation of this study lies in its use of a literature review approach, meaning empirical data do not yet support the findings. Therefore, future research is recommended to conduct quantitative or qualitative empirical testing in the field to validate this conceptual model and to explore the effectiveness of organization-based digital literacy training programs in greater depth.

This study examines how expertise influences the post-editing of translation generated by large language models (LLMs) through the lens of relevant efficiency—the adaptive regulation of effort in response to task demands, which is operationalized here as temporal regulation, intervention calibration, and resource adaptability. We used keystroke logging and mixed-effects modeling to compare student and professional translators who performed full and light post-editing (FPE/LPE) tasks on LLM-generated translations under structured termbase and open-ended Internet-search settings. The findings suggest that post-editing expertise is not necessarily reflected in faster processing, but in how post-editing behavior relates to task requirements. Experts showed a greater increase in time allocation as the density of critical errors increased, indicating more task-sensitive temporal regulation. Expertise-related patterns of error correction varied with post-editing guidelines, while resource conditions were differentially associated with new-error introduction across the two groups. Keystroke-based process indicators also related to editing outcomes, highlighting the importance of evaluating editing activity in relation to its results. These findings support a task-relative understanding of relevant efficiency in the post-editing of LLM-generated translation, suggesting that translator training should prioritize task-sensitive decision-making, temporal regulation, and effective use of external resources rather than processing speed alone.

Frustrated total internal reflection (FTIR) has been used for contact sensing via vision, while repropagated FTIR (RFTIR) has enabled system miniaturization. However, conventional RFTIR-based methods cannot adequately handle overlapping contact images generated by multiple contacts. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach for estimating multiple contacts for multitouch sensing. Images resembling those captured by FTIR-based methods were reconstructed using pseudo-inverse ray tracing, and contact positions were then estimated based on these reconstructions. We evaluated the accuracy of multitouch sensing under various experimental conditions, and confirmed that the estimation was highly accurate, even with four contacts. Several applications were implemented to demonstrate the practicality of the proposed method, including single-sided and simultaneous double-sided multitouch sensing.

Despite the importance of building regulations/codes/standards in the architecture, engineering, and construction industry, the characteristics of its regulation and compliance research are yet to be examined. This study addresses this knowledge gap. Adopting bibliometric, content, and scientometric analyses, as well as inferential statistics, a systematic review of enforcement and compliance with building regulations research from 1990 to 2022 was conducted. The five main research domains found are digital compliance, building energy efficiency and regulations compliance, and natural disaster mitigation through compliance. While there is a strong emphasis on compliance rate/levels and factors domain in various areas such as building daylight regulations, regulatory theories (with a focus on stakeholders and fire protection) have received minimal attention. A framework for future research directions is proposed. Overall, regulation and compliance theories, the benchmarking aspects of regulation, and fire safety require further research. Developed countries are research-active, and the developing ones are inactive. There are linear relationships; for example, as keyword occurrence increases, the total link strength between it and other keywords increases. The more papers journals publish, the more the average number of normalised citations received by the document they publish will increase. The study broadens the horizons of academics, policymakers, and regulators of artificial intelligence in digital compliance of building regulations and building energy efficiency in the climate change crisis. This study is the first detailed evidence and insight into the characteristics of compliance and enforcement of building regulations/codes/standards research. It is also the first of such research on the topic that adopts bibliometric and scientometric analyses, conducts an in-depth and sophisticated visualisation of the characteristics of the literature, and develops a framework for future research directions. Methodologically, the hybrid review methodology in this topic is novel, enabling the limitations of the traditional literature method to be mitigated by the analyses and the in-depth and sophisticated visualisation of the characteristics of the literature. Theoretically, there is extensive and scientific mapping of enforcement and compliance with building regulations research.

Large language models are increasingly used to generate answers with citations in regulatory settings, including compliance review, clinical governance, fiscal assessment, legal interpretation, and institutional risk analysis. Existing work on attribution, retrieval augmented generation, citation evaluation, and sufficient context has clarified when generated claims are grounded in identifiable sources. Regulatory use raises a stricter question. A citation may support an atomic sentence while still failing to justify the regulated conclusion that the system invites a user to accept. This paper develops regulatory evidentiary closure, a conclusion-relative standard for that question, as a formal framework. The framework defines source existence, domain-indexed claim support, and closure as relations over an authorized corpus, cited source set, generated claims, material elements, and regulated conclusion, and states them in explicit notation. Three propositions record the framework’s structure: claim support does not imply closure, metrics restricted to internal model signals cannot determine closure without domain rule structure, and closure checking reduces to a finite coverage problem over material elements. Worked examples from HIPAA security compliance and clinical guideline recommendation show the same failure structure across domains, where a citation supports an atomic claim while the conclusion’s material elements remain uncovered. A coverage matrix then maps seventeen existing evaluation methods against five evidentiary components and shows that none states conclusion-relative closure as an evaluation object. The paper translates the framework into a nine-step reviewer-facing audit protocol and identifies future work on element-mapping reliability, benchmark design, and tool-assisted closure assessment.

documents.abstract: Digital transformation is reshaping modern society, creating opportunities for development while simultaneously generating new forms of inequality, vulnerability and injustice. The study was undertaken because technological advancement does not automatically guarantee equitable participation, rights protection or access to justice, while existing legal responses to emerging digital challenges remain fragmented and largely reactive. The study aims to examine the relationship between digital transformation, equity and justice; analyse the theoretical and legal foundations for addressing emerging digital challenges; and develop an integrated legal pathway for inclusive and just societal transformation. A qualitative doctrinal methodology, complemented by analytical and comparative approaches, was adopted. The study draws on relevant legislation, judicial authorities, scholarly literature and international instruments. The study finds that digital exclusion, algorithmic bias, data privacy violations, cybercrime, platform power and inadequate digital remedies can undermine equity and justice. It further finds that Rawls’ Theory of Justice, Sen’s Capability Approach and Digital Constitutionalism provide complementary foundations for addressing these challenges, but fragmented legal responses remain inadequate. The study consequently proposes the Transformative Digital Justice Framework (TDJF), integrating constitutional rights protection, digital inclusion, responsible technology governance, digital consumer protection, institutional accountability, judicial innovation and inclusive participation. The study concludes that law must move beyond reactive regulation and proactively shape digital transformation to ensure that technological progress advances human dignity, equality, inclusion and justice. Keywords: Digital Transformation; Equity; Justice; Artificial Intelligence; Digital Rights; Consumer Protection; Digital Constitutionalism.

documents.abstract: Organisations increasingly combine employee-led job redesign with artificial intelligence (AI) to support adaptive work and performance. This study examines the relationships among job crafting (JC), self-reported AI use, and employee-reported performance-related outcomes in the UAE public sector. Primary cross-sectional survey data were obtained from 433 employees working in HRM departments of Dubai Government organisations. The study tests the direct associations of JC and AI with the outcome measure, the moderating role of AI in the JC-outcome relationship, and whether these relationships differ formally across gender and age groups. Regression results show positive associations for JC (β = 0.552, p < 0.001) and AI use (β = 0.166, p < 0.001). The AI × JC interaction is not significant (B = −0.024, t = −0.650, p = 0.516), indicating that AI does not strengthen the JC-outcome relationship in this sample. Formal interaction tests also do not establish significant differences in the focal relationships across gender or age groups. The findings suggest that job crafting and AI use may contribute independently to perceived performance-related outcomes, while their combination is not automatically synergistic. The study contributes to human-centred AI and job-crafting research in a public-sector setting, while explicitly recognising limitations arising from convenience sampling, cross-sectional self-report data, and the restricted content validity of the retained measurement composites. From a social sustainability perspective, these findings inform how employee autonomy and responsible AI use may support adaptable public-sector work practices and sustainable human resource management. The results highlight the importance of balancing digital transformation with employee agency, while not establishing long-term sustainability outcomes.

This conceptual paper introduces Reorganization During Absence and Incomplete Positional Restoration, a mechanism by which a person's absence prompts others to redistribute work, responsibilities, and relations of dependence, so that returning does not automatically restore the position previously held. An individual may resume participation in an organization whose arrangements have changed to accommodate the absence. The person's return and the restoration of the former role are therefore separate events. The paper assesses positional restoration by comparing the tasks, relationships, and dependencies that constituted the earlier position with the arrangements in place upon return. It asks which responsibilities moved during the absence, who acquired them, and what would be required to reverse the redistribution. Restoration may be possible, but it requires an additional operation with consequences for those who assumed the work. The mechanism does not establish that the earlier arrangement was preferable, that the returning person is entitled to recover it, or that adaptations made during an absence are necessarily permanent. The documented case concerns New England Patriots quarterback Drew Bledsoe, who was injured during a game against the New York Jets on September 23, 2001. His replacement, Tom Brady, started the following eight games. When Bledsoe was medically cleared to return in November, head coach Bill Belichick retained Brady as the starting quarterback. Belichick explained that preparing both players had reduced the practice opportunities needed by the starter. The starting role and its associated preparation had moved during Bledsoe's absence and were not restored when he became available. A contrasting case concerns Soviet cosmonaut Sergei Krikalev, who launched to the Mir space station in May 1991 and returned in March 1992 after the dissolution of the Soviet Union. His mission was extended because a planned replacement did not assume his duties. Although his circumstances changed substantially during the absence, his assignment had not been transferred to another person and then withheld upon return. Part of the Time, Memory, and Revision series within On Human Modeling, the paper places the mechanism alongside Alfred Schutz's account of the homecomer and examines how continuity of identity differs from continuity of organizational position. Potential applications in human–AI research include organizational transitions, human–AI task allocation, workplace automation, and evaluations of whether restored access or participation also restores the responsibilities, information, and decision authority previously held by a person.

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to draft replies to patient messages, but the methods available for evaluating such drafts were developed for other kinds of systems, and expert evaluators are difficult to recruit at the scale that LLM output requires. We propose Research through Evaluation (RtE), an iterative approach in which the evaluation metrics and the grading rubric are developed together with the clinicians who apply them. We applied RtE in a retrospective comparative study of 158 prostate cancer patient inquiries, comparing replies written by the clinical care team with replies generated by a GPT-4-based in-basket bot. Three rounds of human evaluation with clinical professionals (Rounds 1–3) were followed by a fourth round in which four LLM graders scored the same responses with the final rubric. Across the human rounds, the design moved from disclosed-source comparison to randomized single-blind grading, Conciseness was replaced by Clarity and Trustworthiness by Empathy, and items on editing effort and time to answer were added. In the final clinician evaluation, clinical care team replies scored higher on Completeness, Correctness and Clarity, in-basket bot replies scored higher on Empathy, and in-basket bot replies more often needed major editing. All four LLM graders rated the in-basket bot replies more favourably than the clinical care team replies, and their absolute agreement with one another was low (Krippendorff's alpha 0.07–0.18) compared with that of the clinician graders (0.53–0.81). RtE produced a documented evaluation instrument in which every revision can be traced to the round that prompted it, and the results indicate that zero-shot LLM graders cannot yet replace clinician evaluation in this setting.

documents.abstract: As generative AI becomes increasingly embedded in academic work, it is reshaping how researchers seek, interpret, and use information across scholarly activities (Andersen et al., 2025). At the same time, AI-generated information presents new challenges for credibility assessment because its reliability and suitability for academic tasks are not always readily apparent (Choi et al., 2025). This study examines how generative AI is incorporated into academic information practices and how people respond when its outputs remain uncertain. The semi-structured interviews were conducted with 17 faculty members, graduate students, librarians, and academic support professionals working or studying in U.S. higher-education settings. An iterative thematic analysis showed that participants rarely treated generative AI as a self-contained information source. Instead, they moved between AI systems, scholarly resources, specialised tools, and human expertise as their tasks developed. Uncertainty often emerged when generated information appeared plausible but was difficult to substantiate, when participants lacked the expertise needed to judge an answer, or when AI involvement conflicted with their understanding of appropriate academic work. Participants responded by seeking corroborating evidence, revising how AI was used within a task, or turning away from it when further checking required too much effort or when they wished to retain personal judgement and authorship. Faculty and academic support professionals also described a broader responsibility for helping students and colleagues navigate these uncertainties through clearer expectations and critical guidance. The findings position generative AI within a wider academic information environment and show that its use is shaped by continuing judgements about when generated information is sufficient, when other resources are needed, and where human responsibility should remain.

Amid the rapid evolution of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), this study investigates how integrating this technology into educational feedback processes can enhance learning experiences. Specifically, we investigate the potential of GenAI to complement peer feedback practices among 295 graduate students at a US-based university during the 2023 academic year. Employing an exploratory research design, the study gathered both quantitative and qualitative data through post-course surveys to address key research questions regarding the quality, usefulness, and actionability of peer and AI reviews, as well as their respective advantages and disadvantages. The findings reveal that, while peer reviews were slightly more favorably perceived across all dimensions, AI-generated feedback offered unique strengths, such as consistency and immediacy, which may enrich the feedback experience in distinct ways. The thematic analysis revealed distinct but complementary functions associated with each modality. This research underscores the importance of integrating human expertise with AI technology in feedback mechanisms. By illuminating how AI can augment, rather than replace, human feedback, we offer practical insights for educators, instructional designers, and policymakers seeking to enhance feedback experiences through emerging digital technologies.

Readers of the philosophical literature on artificial intelligence (AI) will encounter an unexpected word, one that medicine has carried for two and a half millennia: pharmakon . Revitalised by Derrida and elaborated by Bernard Stiegler into a general theory of technology, the figure has lately been carried over to generative AI to capture the simultaneous enhancement and diminishment of cognition this technology produces in its users. The present paper argues that when philosophy borrows this word it should borrow it in full, in the sense it has acquired since Plato. The phármakon of contemporary clinical medicine is a relational object whose therapeutic or toxic character emerges in a specified encounter between substance, subject, and context. Stiegler’s pharmacology is itself relational, locating ambivalence in the process of transindividuation; but it does not provide an operational vocabulary for specifying how effects vary systematically between individual subjects. Clinical pharmacology provides such a vocabulary. Its accumulated learning — pharmacokinetic variability, pharmacogenetic polymorphism, idiosyncratic susceptibility, drug–drug interaction, therapeutic window, tolerance, withdrawal, and expectancy effects — has cognitive analogues in human interaction with large language models (LLMs) that have not yet been developed into a coherent pharmacological vocabulary and that early empirical research is beginning to measure. The paper proposes a reframing from the generic to the respondent pharmakon , not as a refutation of Stiegler’s pharmacology but as its specification at a level where clinical, pedagogical, and policy decisions can be made.

Purpose To determine whether retinal foundation-model pretraining reduces the loss of diabetic retinopathy (DR) grading agreement on external fundus-photograph datasets compared with ImageNet-pretrained convolutional networks. Methods RETFound (linear probe and full fine-tuning), EfficientNet-B3 and ResNet-50 were developed on APTOS 2019 (3,662 images) and tested unchanged on Messidor-2 (1,744 images, adjudicated grades) and IDRiD (516 images). The prespecified primary outcome was the difference in internal-to-external quadratic weighted kappa (QWK) drop relative to EfficientNet-B3 for one training run per model; a post hoc analysis averaged three or four runs per model. Results Internal QWK was 0.879 (EfficientNet-B3) and 0.888 (RETFound). In the prespecified analysis, RETFound’s excess drop was + 0.020 (95% CI − 0.024 to + 0.064) on Messidor-2 and + 0.033 (− 0.023 to + 0.091) on IDRiD; averaged over runs, it was + 0.068 (+ 0.003 to + 0.134; Holm p = 0.074) and + 0.020 (− 0.041 to + 0.080). On Messidor-2, referable-DR sensitivity was 36–43% with specificity 90–98%, and EfficientNet-B3 graded 259 of 270 mild-DR images as no DR. Matching case mix and merging grades 0 and 1 reduced the Messidor-2 drop by 63–69%. Label smoothing reproduced RETFound’s lower external calibration error. Conclusion Retinal foundation-model pretraining did not reduce external performance loss. Similar internal agreement did not establish robustness across image sources and reference standards, and no model was suitable for autonomous screening at these operating points.

Petrophysical rock typing (PRT) is the cornerstone of reservoir characterization, bridging microscopic pore-throat morphology and macroscopic dynamic flow behavior to control hydrocarbon-in-place estimates, saturation–height functions, and numerical simulation grid-block properties. For over five decades, reservoir workflows have relied on conventional frameworks rooted in capillary pressure curves (Leverett, 1941; Thomeer, 1960), pore-throat size calibrations (Winland R₃₅; Pittman, 1992), and the modified Kozeny-Carman formulation, most notably the Reservoir Quality Index (RQI) and Flow Zone Indicator (FZI) proposed by Amaefule et al. (1993). However, these classical formulations frequently struggle in complex carbonate systems, tight gas sandstones, and multi-modal reservoirs due to fundamental physical limitations, including the conflation of static capillary storage with dynamic flow capacity, non-Darcy flow regimes, and unresolved multi-scale heterogeneity. This review systematically traces the methodological evolution of rock typing from its historical foundations to the contemporary ascent of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML). We first evaluate advanced conventional advancements that address classical shortcomings, including the rigorous decoupling of Petrophysical Static Rock Types (PSRT) from Petrophysical Dynamic Rock Types (PDRT), the calibration of effective flow porosity (PHIZ) via Purcell-PSKT porosimetry, and fractal bound-water models for low-permeability rocks. We then conduct an in-depth critical analysis of data-driven AI, examining how unsupervised clustering (Self-Organizing Maps, K-Means, Fuzzy C-Means, DBSCAN) automates electrofacies discovery from multi-well wireline logs, and how supervised tree-based ensembles (Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM) and deep architectures predict rock classes and continuous permeability. Crucially, we highlight the paradigm shift toward Physics-Informed Machine Learning (PIML), where non-Darcy flow physics and mass conservation are embedded directly into loss functions, and Explainable AI (SHAP, LIME) is leveraged to eliminate black-box opacity. We further analyze the revolution in Digital Rock Physics (DRP) and Image-based Microscale Rock Typing (IMRT), which combines micro-CT, FIB-SEM, and deep learning segmentation (PRRT and TSRT) with Lattice Boltzmann flow simulation to provide verifiable ground truth. Finally, we replace speculative risks with an industry-grounded audit of genuine operational pitfalls in AI petrophysics — including spatial autocorrelation data leakage, out-of-distribution extrapolation failure, core-to-log depth-matching errors, and regulatory compliance — and synthesize these insights into a unified, multi-scale, physics-informed digital rock typing roadmap for resilient reservoir modeling.

One proposed mechanism for human planning is the mental simulation, or “rollout,” of potential action sequences to evaluate future outcomes. While rollout-based models have seen great success in artificial intelligence, cognitive models that describe how people use rollouts remain scarce, in part because they are difficult to fit to behavioral data. Existing methods rely on computationally intensive simulations that result in approximate, noisy estimates of latent planning parameters. We introduce ROSETTE (Rollouts with Stochastic Early Termination and Tractable Estimation), a rollout-based model for finite goal-directed tasks with absorbing goals that provides analytically tractable, simulation-free model fitting. ROSETTE treats planning as a sequence of mental simulations formalized as an absorbing Markov chain. The model deterministically accumulates analytically computed expected rollout evidence and performs a variable number of policy-update cycles. We fit ROSETTE to data from human participants in two multi-step planning tasks and found that it well accounted for a rich set of summary statistics of behavior. By making this specific class of absorbing-goal rollout models tractable, our framework provides a testable account of how people may simulate and evaluate possible futures.

Background/Objectives: Evidence on how Romanian dental students use generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is limited. This study assessed academic GenAI use, perceived educational and clinical usefulness, self-reported trust, ethical concerns, and attitudes toward curricular integration and institutional guidance. Methods: A cross-sectional paper-based survey was administered on 12 and 13 February 2026 to fourth- and fifth-year dental students attending scheduled teaching activities at one Romanian university. Of 192 eligible students, 167 attended the recruitment sessions, 155 responded (92.8%), and 148 were analysed. The study-specific questionnaire underwent expert content review but not psychometric validation. Spearman correlations, the Wilcoxon signed-rank test, and a supplementary chi-square test were applied with Holm correction across 18 tests; open-ended answers underwent descriptive thematic analysis. Results: Overall, 41.2% of students used GenAI frequently or very frequently. Use frequency correlated weakly to moderately with perceived understanding, time-saving, academic performance, and educational value (ρ = 0.25–0.51). ChatGPT received higher usefulness ratings for learning dental concepts than AI in general received for clinical decision-making (median 4 vs. 3; p < 0.001), although the items referred to different AI applications. Trust correlated moderately with perceived educational value (ρ = 0.49). Privacy and critical-thinking concerns correlated moderately with support for institutional guidelines (ρ = 0.36 and 0.46), whereas critical-thinking concern was unrelated to support for curricular integration. Conclusions: Students regarded GenAI mainly as an educational aid and were cautious about its clinical use. Structured training in critical appraisal and ethical use, supported by institutional policy, appears warranted. The associations are cross-sectional and may not generalise beyond this sample.

documents.abstract: Background Clinical agentic artificial intelligence (AI) can alter its actions during a clinical task, creating failure pathways that conventional performance metrics may not capture. Whether safeguards interrupt these pathways remains uncertain. Aim To map safeguard effects, residual failures, human recovery, and resource consequences in clinical agentic and related AI workflows. Methods We searched PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, and IEEE Xplore, for English-language, peer-reviewed empirical journal reports. This scoping review used independent screening, duplicate extraction, narrative synthesis, and result-specific critical appraisal. Results The 111 reports comprised 56 functionally agentic, 29 related non-agentic, 22 architecture-uncertain, and four human-factors reports; 38 of the 56 agentic reports explicitly documented model-directed subsequent-action selection. Among the 111 selected appraisal results, none both isolated a specified safeguard’s effect and demonstrated reduced measured patient harm. Configurations incorporating safeguards improved selected outcomes, but gains coexisted with omissions, reduced sensitivity, false reassurance, delay, or transferred review burden. Concurrent changes in models, prompts, evidence access, and workflow frequently prevented attribution to individual controls. Some patient-randomised trials reported patient or process benefits, but evaluated bundled interventions rather than the contribution of a safeguard. Human authority was more often documented than successful error detection and recovery; requiring clinician approval did not establish that residual errors were recognised and corrected. Performance varied across models, settings, and information conditions, limiting transfer of favourable findings. Reported efficiency gains depended on measurement boundaries and did not consistently account for review, correction, escalation, and downstream work. Discussion The evidence exposes a gap between local error control and safety across a complete clinical episode. A safeguard can reduce a targeted error while shifting risk to later decisions or human reviewers. We propose a post hoc , non-ordinal evidence profile addressing mechanism fidelity, residual and introduced failures, robustness, joint human–AI performance, and clinical consequences. The profile requires validation; heterogeneous designs and retrospective methodological refinements constrain inference. Conclusion Clinical safety should be evaluated across the complete care pathway, tracing safeguard effects through residual error, human recovery, and patient-relevant outcomes. Selective autonomy requires joint assessment of residual risk and the capacity for timely human review.

documents.abstract: Occupational health risks are common among oil and gas dispensing workers, making safety training an important component of workplace health protection. This study examined the relationship between safety training and health-seeking behaviour among oil and gas dispensing workers in Calabar Metropolis, Cross River State, Nigeria. A cross-sectional research design was adopted, and data were collected from 212 oil and gas dispensing workers using a structured questionnaire. Safety training and health-seeking behaviour were measured using composite scores derived from Likert-type items. Descriptive statistics were used to assess the extent of safety training practices, while Pearson Product Moment Correlation and simple linear regression were employed to examine the relationship and predictive effect of safety training on health-seeking behaviour. The findings indicated a high level of safety training among the workers. A strong, positive and statistically significant relationship was found between safety training and health-seeking behaviour (r = .775, p < .001). Regression analysis further showed that safety training significantly and positively predicted health-seeking behaviour (B = 0.685, β = .776, t = 17.842, p < .001). The regression model was statistically significant, F(1, 210) = 318.354, p < .001, and explained 60.3% of the variance in health-seeking behaviour (R² = .603). The study concludes that higher levels of safety training are associated with more positive health-seeking behaviour among oil and gas dispensing workers. It recommends sustained and periodic safety training incorporating hazard recognition, preventive health practices, early reporting of health problems and appropriate utilisation of healthcare services. Practically, the study provides evidence for integrating health-seeking components into routine safety training, particularly early recognition and reporting of occupational health problems, preventive practices, and appropriate utilisation of healthcare services. Keywords: Safety training; Health-seeking behaviour; Occupational health; oil and gas workers; Calabar Metropolis.

documents.abstract: Screen sharing in online conferencing can unintentionally expose private information on the presenter’s screen. Existing protections mainly rely on masking or blurring, which can disrupt context and interaction understanding. We propose a generative, semantic-aware replacement approach that substitutes sensitive regions with visually coherent content in dynamic screen environments. We implement two variants with different degrees of semantic grounding: Semantic-Element-Preserving Replacement (SEPR) and Semantic-Element-Agnostic Replacement (SEAR), and compare them with masking and blurring. In a video-based user study that isolates latency effects, we evaluate detectability, confidence of detection, perceived identifiability, and user experience from both screen-sharer and screen-viewer perspectives. SEAR significantly reduced detectability relative to masking, and also lowered perceived identifiability compared to blurring and SEPR. Replacement methods significantly improved context understanding and visual naturalness over masking, and SEAR also outperformed blurring in visual naturalness; for context preservation, SEAR was rated higher than masking, while the SEPR–masking comparison was near the significance threshold. Qualitative responses further revealed role-dependent concerns and a social risk of misinterpretation, motivating design implications for tuning semantic fidelity and signaling obfuscation intent.

The use of inter-organizational information systems (such as cloud computing environments, data markets and sup-ply chains) provides organizations with the ability to manage their activities together and generate value from those shared activities. However, while technical controls are important to limit the spread of damage caused by unauthor-ized actions taken by employees within the organization, technical controls cannot prevent the consequences of em-ployees acting outside of established policies or the absence of effective organizational governance. A single over-permissive policy or configuration error can affect multiple organizations that are part of the same network and lead to loss of trust among those organizations and non-compliance with regulations. To address the need for a compre-hensive sociotechnical framework for understanding how behavior, technical controls and institutional governance influence the exposure of organizations to risk, we developed the Collaborative Security Alignment (CSA) model based upon Orlikowski's duality of technology, Protection Motivation Theory and Task-Technology Fit. The CSA model proposes that: (a) Technical controls are a prerequisite for protecting organization resources but are not suffi-cient; (b) Organizational culture and behavioral nudges influence the effectiveness of technical controls; and (c) Inter-organizational governance (via contracts, auditing and common metrics) contributes to long-term resiliency. We used a convergent mixed methods approach to assess the validity of the CSA model. We conducted a survey of 210 IS professionals and analyzed the data using Structural Equation Modeling (SEM); we completed three case studies and analyzed them using thematic analysis; and we created a novel, reproducible simulation that compares a rule-based baseline to a CSA toolkit consisting of machine learning-based anomaly detection, workflow-embedded policy nudges, tiered access governance, and shared auditing. Our SEM analysis supported each of our four hypoth-eses. Our simulation results indicated that when all components of the CSA toolkit were applied collectively, the aggregate exposure to vulnerabilities was reduced by approximately 67 percent compared to the baseline (range of sectors was 56-80%). Since the reduction in exposure to vulnerability is dependent on the assumptions made con-cerning the effects of each component of the CSA toolkit, we provide ablation and sensitivity analyses (results var-ied from 58-75 percent across the tested ranges) and consider the findings as a demonstration of the model's capabil-ities as opposed to empirical evidence. We conclude our paper with recommendations for managers and discussions of algorithmic fairness, ethical considerations related to conducting research and cross-jurisdictional regulatory compliance issues.

As Large Language Model (LLM)-based agents increasingly make decisions and take actions for users, understanding how transparency shapes human–agent interaction is critical. We report a controlled study with 60 participants interacting with a policy-governed agent in a customer-service domain under three transparency conditions: opaque, partial, and transparent. The study shows greater transparency increased perceived understanding of agent behavior. However, it did not improve identification of silent failures, defined as plausible errors presented without warning. Partial transparency supported error detection more effectively than full transparency, suggesting that additional explanations do not necessarily enhance critical evaluation. Greater transparency was also associated with lower perceived agent steerability, reflecting reduced belief that outcomes could be influenced through altered response strategies. Participants challenged agent decisions less directly and engaged more with stated rules under transparent conditions. These findings highlight trade-offs between clarity, oversight, and user agency, motivating transparency designs that better support effective human oversight.

documents.abstract: Background Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is embedded in nursing students' routines, yet academic AI overreliance is rarely quantified, especially in resource-limited settings. Objective To examine the relationship between self-perceived academic AI overreliance and academic performance among nursing students in the West Bank, Palestine. Methods A multicentre, cross-sectional correlational study was conducted with 1213 second- to fourth-year nursing students from 11 Palestinian universities who completed the 22-item Academic AI Overreliance Scale (AAIO) and the 8-item Academic Performance Scale (AP). The relationship between self-perceived academic AI overreliance and academic performance was estimated using hierarchical regression analysis, with sociodemographic and academic characteristics being entered in the first step, and academic AI overreliance being added in the second step. Results The mean age of participants was 21.79 years (SD = 1.09; range 20–25 years), and 676 of them (55.7%) were female. The self-perceived academic AI overreliance in the study was moderate (mean = 2.42, SD = 0.49). Higher self-perceived academic AI overreliance was associated with higher self-reported academic performance (r = 0.34, p < 0.001); this self-perceived academic AI overreliance was the associated factor (β = 0.35, p < 0.001). Conclusions Self-perceived academic AI overreliance was common yet moderate; its positive association with academic performance underscores the need to shape AI engagement and safeguard unassisted learning. The findings give nurse educators a measurable target for AI-literacy curricula, assessment design and institutional policy in a resource-limited setting.

documents.abstract: Background Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in healthcare and medical education. We described self-reported AI familiarity, use, and attitudes among students, faculty, and staff at a medical college in the United Arab Emirates to inform local training. Methods We conducted a cross-sectional online survey from August to October 2025. Study-specific composite summary scores ranged from 0 to 100. Linear models adjusted for respondent group, sex, and age, with HC3 standard errors. Sensitivity analyses examined AI use scoring, bootstrap confidence intervals, and restricted-age group comparisons. Results After four blank records were excluded, 375 respondents remained; the estimated participation proportion was 34.7%. At least one use of a generative AI tool during the previous three months was reported by 96.8% of respondents, whereas 78.1% reported AI use specifically in academic studies or professional practice. Formal AI training was reported by 10.8%. Mean AI familiarity, AI use, and AI attitude scores were 61.6, 62.9, and 72.1. Adjusted student-versus-faculty/staff differences were 1.91 points for AI familiarity (95% confidence interval [CI] -6.99 to 10.81), -2.87 for AI use (95% CI -23.17 to 17.43), and 2.32 for AI attitude (95% CI -5.43 to 10.07). Because age overlap between students and faculty/staff was limited, these adjusted group estimates may partly rely on extrapolation and should not be interpreted as age-matched comparisons. Average linear-model age associations indicated lower AI familiarity and higher AI attitude scores. The adjusted male-versus-female AI use estimate was uncertain (-7.61, 95% CI -16.14 to 0.92). The higher adjusted AI attitude score among male respondents was exploratory and requires caution because no multiplicity adjustment was applied. Training-stage comparisons were exploratory and showed no consistent pattern. The restricted-age analysis included 59 respondents and had wide confidence intervals. Conclusions Any recent generative AI use was common, while formal training was uncommon. These findings may guide local teaching on responsible AI use, checking AI-generated information, and maintaining human oversight. Self-report, one institution, and study-specific scores that were not formally validated limit interpretation. Future studies should validate the measures and include objective assessments of AI competency.

documents.abstract: Assistive indoor mobile robots are increasingly expected to connect natural-language requests about familiar places and objects with the metric maps used for localization and motion planning. Metric simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) supports reliable geometry and collision avoidance, whereas many open-vocabulary scene-graph systems remain separated from the navigation stacks used on deployed robots. This paper presents a semantic-topological cognitive map (STCM) that bridges these representations for assistive navigation. The system derives place nodes from a LiDAR–inertial pose stream through a dual growing neural gas backend and consolidates object instances over time. GroundingDINO and MobileSAM provide open-vocabulary semantic grounding in the map frame through LiDAR–image association and temporal score fusion. A tool-mediated large language model interface maps user commands to explicit STCM nodes, while graph search and ROS 2 Navigation2 (Nav2) remain responsible for path computation and execution. Evaluation with recorded robot sessions, an outdoor distribution-shift probe, and a public indoor-scene benchmark indicates that the STCM backend improves object-graph construction and that the language interface improves functional-command grounding when requested objects are recoverable by perception. The pipeline is demonstrated on a Ranger Garden Assistant platform with FAST-LIO2 mapping, incremental graph construction during the mapping pass, and waypoint execution from a serialized map artifact.

Geometry education in South Africa’s Senior Phase has been marked by low learner attainment and a disconnect between the potential of artificial intelligence (AI) tools and their classroom use. Despite global advances, educators’ readiness to integrate AI in this context has remained underexplored. This study examined Senior Phase mathematics educators’ perceptions of integrating AI tools into geometry teaching. It focused on perceived benefits, implementation barriers, and the role of professional development in enabling meaningful use. A qualitative case study design was employed within a constructivist paradigm. Nine purposively selected educators from urban schools in the Free State and Gauteng participated in semi-structured interviews. Data were analysed thematically using a hybrid deductive–inductive approach. Educators showed cautious optimism, identifying improved visualisation, time efficiency, and support for differentiated learning. However, implementation was constrained by infrastructural instability, limited device access, curriculum pressures, and lack of subject-specific training. The use of AI remained largely confined to lesson preparation, and concerns about cognitive surrender emerged. The findings indicated that AI integration was constrained less by technology than by systemic and pedagogical limitations. Professional development emerged as the decisive factor shaping classroom use. Artificial intelligence was also identified as enabling educator inclusion in the case of a participant with a physical disability. Contribution: This study contributed by framing cognitive surrender as a risk in geometry learning, by positioning professional development as the decisive mediating variable between AI perceptions and classroom practice, and by foregrounding AI as a tool of professional equity for educators with disabilities. These findings contribute to the current research and developments in mathematics education at both the national and international levels by addressing the improvement of mathematics teaching and learning in the South African Senior Phase.

Multisensory XR may support autistic adults, yet sensory-friendly design often prioritizes less input. We conducted a mixed-methods, counterbalanced within-subjects study with 20 Chinese autistic adults evaluating five complete XR configurations presenting identical science content: text (L1), text with images (L2), click-triggered spatial audio (L3), gradual light and audio (L4), and L4 plus vibrotactile and thermal cues (L5). The measure combined comfort (Q1), absence of sensory discomfort (Q2), and liking (Q3). Evaluations differed (Friedman χ 2 (4) = 46.39, p <.001, Kendall’s W =.58), and a Q1–Q2 analysis retained the omnibus difference. L3 was lowest ( M = 2.97/5; tied lowest for 16/20). L5 was highest descriptively ( M = 4.43/5), but corrected comparisons did not distinguish it from L1 or L4, and ceiling compression constrained superiority claims. Participants valued clarity, self-pacing, gradual transitions, exit options, and coordinated cues, while disliking abruptness, simultaneous demands, and insufficient warning. These configuration-level findings identify participant-described dimensions for controlled studies.

Serendipity, the discovery of unexpected yet valuable items, has become an important objective for recommender systems (RS) aiming to reduce filter bubbles and support long-term user satisfaction. Although accuracy-driven models predict known preferences effectively, they can restrict exploration and reinforce narrow consumption patterns. Despite increasing attention to serendipity as a beyond-accuracy objective, the field remains fragmented because definitions, evaluation protocols, and ethical considerations are not consistently aligned. This systematic review examines serendipity in RS from 2020 to 2025, covering 147 studies and 98 algorithmic contributions. We synthesize diverse definitions into a unified conceptual framework centred on relevance, novelty, and unexpectedness. We also present a methodological taxonomy that traces the field’s evolution from heuristic and traditional approaches to deep learning, knowledge graph, generative, and LLM-based methods. Reported results show that recent LLM-based approaches can achieve strong performance on serendipity-oriented tasks, with $$\:NDC{G}_{seren}$$ scores of up to 0.398. We further review evaluation practices and highlight the gap between computational proxies and subjective user experience. Through quantitative ethical analysis, we show that 74.1% of studies acknowledge ethical concerns, but only 6.8% include dedicated ethics sections, 19.7% operationalize ethical metrics, and 5.4% address content safety. By integrating conceptual, methodological, evaluative, and ethical perspectives, this review provides guidance for developing serendipity-oriented RS that balance relevance with beneficial discovery.

Little is known about how young prospective users of robo-advisors form their views of them. This study examines how service awareness and social influence relate to perceived ease of use (PEOU), perceived usefulness (PU) and the intention to use robo-advisors among Generation Z adults in India. Responses from 246 respondents aged 18–28 years, collected online through business-school networks in February 2024, were analysed with partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM) and confirmatory factor analysis. Service awareness was associated with PEOU (β = 0.387) but not with PU beyond PEOU (β = 0.056, 95% CI [− 0.035, 0.155]). Social influence was associated with both PEOU (β = 0.358) and PU (β = 0.276) and, in an exploratory extended model, directly with intention (β = 0.322). PEOU was associated with intention in every specification. The association between PU and intention was not robust: it was significant in the hypothesised PLS-SEM model (β = 0.291) but not in the covariance-based estimate of that model or, in the exploratory extended model, after the direct path from social influence was added (β = 0.118, 95% CI [− 0.099, 0.327]). PEOU and PU were distinct but closely related (latent correlation 0.883, 95% CI [0.806, 0.943]). Method-factor models did not reach admissible solutions, so method variance could not be quantified. The design is cross-sectional and the sample is a convenience sample, so the estimates are associations for young adults reached through business-school networks, not for rural, non-student or older investors. Trust in algorithms was not measured.

The rapid diffusion of generative artificial intelligence (GAI) across teaching, learning, and research demands institutional approaches that are ethical, transparent, and scalable. This study posed the questions: what guiding questions should shape a scalable framework for the ethical use of GAI in educational institutions? Drawing on preliminary results from an ongoing exploratory survey organized around seven categories of GAI engagement, namely: GAI-Powered, GAI-Generated, GAI-Modified, GAI-Revised, GAI-Assembled, GAI-Summarized, and GAI-Rewritten. Respondents consistently emphasized need for human validation, transparency, and attribution as non-negotiable. These findings aligned with international standards and professional guidance (ALA, ACRL and UNESCO etcetera) relevant to higher education and librarianship. The preliminary data from this pilot study included responses from eight participants including students, faculty, and staff across targeted population (education). Based on the results, the guiding questions enabled the proposed framework to address pedagogical, documentation, equity & privacy concerns surrounding ethical use of generative artificial intelligence in educational.

documents.abstract: Purpose Investigations of job characteristics often include an a priori classification of these job elements as either resources or demands. The purpose of this paper was to examine variability in appraisals of job characteristics with respect to perception as resource and/or demand, differential association with positive and negative outcomes and the potential buffering effect of resources on the relationships between demands and negative work outcomes. Design/methodology/approach A sample of 568 working respondents recruited from Prolific completed an online survey. They were asked to think only about their primary job and each administered survey branched content dependent on whether their job could be described as consisting of the different Occupational Information Network (O*NET) job characteristics. Workers also rated the level of resource, challenging demand and hindering demand for each relevant job characteristic. Findings Results support the assertion that job characteristics are not uniquely categorized as a resource or demand, but rather, what is viewed as challenging is also commonly interpreted as resourceful. Furthermore, greater experienced resources moderate the challenge–engagement relationship as well as the hindrance-stress and hindrance–burnout relationships. Originality/value The authors polled a diverse collection of job types across industries who responded to a broad set of characteristics derived from O*NET specifications. They additionally explored characteristics at two levels of aggregation (retaining O*NET category groupings), which again expands their collective knowledge of how employees experience resources, challenges and hindrances within different work domains, as well as the consequences of these experiences.

Large language model (LLM) chatbots are increasingly consulted for dental decisions, but case-by-case accuracy does not show whether their advice changes when, and only when, a clinically decisive fact changes. Metamorphic testing checks whether answers to two nearly identical cases relate as clinical rules require, without defining a single correct answer for each case. We applied it to oral and maxillofacial surgery and emergency dental decision-making. Thirty guideline-anchored relations were locked before querying, and 60 synthetic case pairs differing in one variable were submitted with a structured prompt to the ChatGPT (GPT-6 Astra) and Gemini (Gemini 3.8) web interfaces. Two blinded specialists scored each pair, with blinded adjudication of disagreements. In the main analysis (58 pairs; two defective vignettes withdrawn), relations were violated in 0 ChatGPT and 8 Gemini pairs (13.8%; p = 0.016, accounting for clustering within relations); with all 60 pairs, 1 vs. 8 (p = 0.063). Gemini violations clustered at numerical thresholds, escalation red flags and a sex-label invariance relation, and 13 of 116 Gemini responses, but no ChatGPT response, contained a safety violation. Chatbots that appear competent case by case can fail at clinically decisive thresholds; metamorphic testing offers a reproducible audit before clinical use.
