documents.abstract: Poor diet is among the leading modifiable causes of non-communicable disease, and the urban food environment through which commercial actors supply, price, place and promote food is increasingly recognised as a principal pathway linking commercial practices to population nutrition. At the same time, cities are adopting smart city informatics, the integrated use of geospatial, sensor, mobility, transaction, platform and artificial intelligence data to monitor and govern urban systems. Whether these informatics can help mitigate the commercial determinants of poor nutrition, rather than simply describing or even amplifying them, has not been critically examined. This critical narrative review appraises peer-reviewed and institutional literature published between January 2010 and September 2026, identified through structured searching of biomedical and multidisciplinary indexes, citation chasing and institutional sources. Evidence was organised around four questions: how informatics conceptualise and measure urban food environments, what such measurement can and cannot reveal about diet and health, which informatics-enabled approaches have been used to regulate commercial practices, and what governance conditions shape their legitimacy and equity. The synthesis indicates that informatics have substantially improved the scale, temporal resolution and spatial specificity of food environment measurement, particularly through mobility traces, street-level imagery, online food delivery platform data and automated detection of marketing. Associations between measured environments and diet nonetheless remain modest and inconsistent, reflecting exposure misclassification, residential self-selection and the dominance of cross-sectional designs. The strongest evidence of benefit comes not from informatics alone but from regulatory interventions, such as advertising restrictions, planning controls and fiscal measures, whose evaluation was made possible by commercial purchase data and administrative records. Major unresolved problems include dependence on proprietary corporate data, weak validation of machine-learning classifiers, neglect of informal and digital food retail in low- and middle-income countries, and the risk that smart city partnerships reproduce the commercial influence they are intended to counter. Informatics are therefore best understood as enabling infrastructure for accountability and policy evaluation rather than as interventions in their own right. Public data stewardship, transparent validation standards and quasi-experimental evaluation of platform-level regulation are identified as priorities for research and practice.
topics: Global Public Health Policies and Epidemiology

documents.abstract: Detection of plant diseases properly and at the right time is one way of securing the food production process, saving costs and applying chemicals in an inappropriate manner. There have been some advancements made in the area of Deep Learning (DL) that have improved the process of automated diagnosis of plant disease. But most of these systems do not take into consideration the treatment methods that are sustainable. This systematic review examines the present status of Smart Plant Disease Detection Systems (SPDDS) through the application of deep learning techniques along with the adoption of organic solutions in disease detection and management process. For this purpose, a robust review methodology has been used including 102 articles that have been published from 2015 to 2025, focusing on CNNs, Optimization Techniques (GA/PSO) and IoT & Mobile System. Organic treatments for plant diseases have been examined as well in relation to its integration with artificial intelligence technology in diagnosis. In this study, different models have been compared on the basis of accuracy, F1 score, scalability, sustainability of treatment and real-time processing capability.

Street lighting accounts for a significant share of municipal electricity consumption, and most installations still operate at full brightness from dusk to dawn regardless of road activity. This paper presents a smart street light system that adjusts lamp intensity according to real-time road activity. Video frames from a roadside camera are processed by a lightweight deep-learning object detector to recognize pedestrians and vehicles; a tracking module assigns persistent identities and estimates movement direction; and a rule-based controller converts the detected activity into a pulse-widthmodulation (PWM) dimming command for an LED driver. When the road is empty, the lamp holds a low baseline level that satisfies minimum safety requirements, and it ramps up when a pedestrian or vehicle is detected in, or approaching, its zone. Two candidate designs were compared, and a detector-plus-tracker pipeline was selected for its balance of accuracy and real-time performance on edge hardware. The selected design reaches 92.6 percent precision and 89.4 percent recall with 34.2 ms inference latency, and the estimated energy saving over constant-output lighting ranges from 34.5 to 65.6 percent depending on traffic density. The work shows that vision-driven adaptive lighting can reduce energy use while preserving road safety and provides a scalable basis for smart-city lighting.

documents.abstract: The global tobacco epidemic affects the well-being, health, and development of millions of people. While recent advances have greatly improved smoking behaviors monitoring, there remains a lack of widely acceptable, low-power, unobtrusive smoking behaviors monitoring way in real-world scenarios. In this paper, we present SMART ( S moking M onitoring with A coustic Sensing and Sequence R ecognition T echnology)-Glasses, a low-power and minimally obtrusive system that leverages both active and passive acoustic modalities on smart glasses to monitor smoking behavior or recognize the action of lighting a cigarette which enables timely detection, adapting to different user needs. SMART-Glasses innovatively utilizes two speakers and one microphone mounted on the lower rim of the eyeglass frame to emit ultrasonic signals and capture the resulting echoes and passive sounds, thereby extracting features related to smoking behaviors. Furthermore, we introduce a gated sensing enhancement model that amplifies smoking-related features across various noisy conditions. Finally, a smoking action sequence recognition model captures temporal dependencies, allowing the system to distinguish smoking behavior sequences from irrelevant actions. SMART-Glasses is designed for ordinary users who wish to quit smoking and is intended for use in naturalistic environments such as homes, offices, and outdoor areas. Evaluation in both lab and semi-wild settings demonstrates high performance in recognizing lighting and smoking behaviors, showing strong potential for real-world deployment.

Social media is a key concept in contemporary political science.Since the first tweet in 2006, social media has flourished.The emergence of a range of platforms including X, Facebook, YouTube, WhatsApp, Instagram, and TikTok has changed how everyday individuals and political actors communicate and interact.Its impact has been felt worldwide, across the Americas, Europe, Africa, and Asia, and in the context of elections, strategic communication, agenda setting, protests, and youth political participation.It has also been strongly implicated in democratic erosion.As concerns over its negative impacts grow, conversations turn to how "social media" might be utilized and regulated-by whom-and its political implications. Conceptualizing Social MediaWhile its use is ubiquitous, "there is no one definition of 'social media'" (Ellison & Hardey, 2014, p. 24).Over the last 10 years, three overlapping conceptualizations of social media have developed, shaping how we study, interpret, and respond to it.First, it has been conceptualized as a technical tool; second, as a sociotechnical system in which technology shapes and is shaped by human behavior (Latour, 2005); and third, as an ecosystemic network with interconnec ted and hybrid characteristics.

Haptic feedback on smartphones relies predominantly on Linear Resonant Actuators (LRAs), which operate efficiently only near their resonant frequency and cannot reproduce the broadband vibrations (100–1,000 Hz) required for realistic texture rendering. We present SonicHaptics, a method that repurposes the built-in speaker of a commodity smartphone as a haptic actuator, transmitting airborne vibrations through a fingertip contact piece to render surface textures without additional hardware. The system incorporates a dynamic frequency correction mechanism that tracks finger sliding velocity in real time, enabling texture presentation synchronized with natural exploratory movements. A technical evaluation across four smartphones (iPhone 13, iPhone 15 Pro Max, Pixel 5, and Galaxy S24 Ultra) demonstrates that built-in speakers consistently provide broadband vibration output spanning 100–1,000 Hz, whereas vibration actuators are confined to narrow-band operation. A user study ( N = 30) comparing speaker-based rendering against vibration-actuator-based rendering using three materials with distinct frequency-band characteristics (0–100 Hz, 100–300 Hz, and 300–1,000 Hz) shows that the speaker-based method yields significantly higher realism ratings across all tested bands on the evaluated device, with the largest improvements for mid- and high-frequency textures. Our results establish that repurposing smartphone speakers for haptic rendering is a viable, hardware-free approach to broadband texture presentation on commodity mobile devices.

Speaking anxiety is common and can be influenced by visual cues such as gaze and body language. While many coping strategies focus on preparation ( before speaking) or reflection ( after speaking), our work investigates real-time support delivered in the moment ( during speaking). We present SpeakAR, a real-time intervention that uses head-worn holographic augmented reality (AR) to reshape how speakers view their listeners. SpeakAR introduces two strategies: Audience-Augmentation (AA), which adds virtual elements while preserving audience visibility, and Audience-Occlusion (AO), which reduces access to evaluative audience cues. In an exploratory within-subjects study with 18 participants, we measured speaking anxiety through self-reported distress and acoustic speech features (e.g., jitter, pause rate), and evaluated speech performance through self- and observer-rated assessments. While AA produced mixed effects, AO showed lower anxiety measures and higher observer-rated performance than baseline. These findings highlight AR’s potential to provide support during in-person speaking while revealing trade-offs between anxiety reduction and access to social feedback.

The rapid adoption of Large Language Models (LLMs) confronts document-intensive public administration with structural changes that impact cognitive work processes and place new demands on staff. This exploratory, qualitative study examines the effects of this technological deployment on the competence profiles of employees in Swiss cantonal and municipal administrations. Based on eight semi-structured expert interviews with HR and digitalization executives, the study draws a nuanced picture of de-skilling, up-skilling, and re-skilling processes. While the automation of routine tasks jeopardizes traditional entry-level positions (de-skilling) and threatens to erode domain knowledge – which is becoming increasingly vital for evaluation and accountability over the longer term – LLMs bring about a perceived increase in autonomy and self-efficacy at the individual level (up-skilling). Contrary to the hypothesis of «metacognitive laziness» frequently postulated in the literature, the dissonance between algorithmic probabilism and the rule-of-law zero-tolerance policy for errors demands an elevation of higher-order thinking skills (re-skilling). The core human contribution shifts from pure text generation toward higher-order thinking skills, requiring verification and accountability skills within human-in-the-loop frameworks. Institutionally, a paradoxical, technology-induced workload inflation is also evident: technological time savings in text production are neutralized by a rising volume of longer, AI-generated external inquiries as well as higher qualitative demands, meaning that the anticipated reduction in workload for staff fails to materialize. The article concludes with strategic recommendations for the proactive and legally compliant management of this socio-technical transformation process.

Recent surveys show that only 1 in 400 startups secure funding and achieve post-fund sustainability. Startup assessment is becoming increasingly complicated due to the evolving entrepreneurial landscape, which is affected by too many factors, compelling venture capital firms to harness state-of-the-art Artificial Intelligence (AI). Natural Language Processing (NLP) offers a promising approach for startup assessment, by analyzing documents that summarize key factors of long-term success. Although startup sustainability research is active, modern NLP for assessing business plans has received limited attention. Specifically, the majority of previous works consider only short text descriptions of startups instead of complete business plans, and do not offer adaptability to the varying investment criteria of different investors. In this paper, we propose ForeStart, a startup sustainability forecasting system powered by a transformer-based language model that offers seamless adaptability to the particular needs of users. The proposed system can analyze business plans of unlimited length, including also startup-related content such as pitch deck presentations and company websites. ForeStart is based on a hierarchical Distilled Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers–Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (DistilBERT–BiLSTM) architecture trained using both unsupervised domain adaptation and supervised learning, effectively leveraging both unlabeled and labeled business plans. In addition, the proposed system addresses issues arising from privacy concerns and low-resource settings of the startup environment. Our experiments on actual business plans achieve 79% $$F_{1}$$ score in forecasting startup sustainability, even with a limited number of labeled business plans as training data. As an assisting screening tool for analysts, ForeStart can significantly reduce the time required for startup assessments, providing value to Venture Capital (VC) organizations. Moreover, startup founders can also use ForeStart for self-assessment.

Leading research laboratories name artificial general intelligence (AGI) as their goal, yet there is no generally accepted definition of AGI, nor an agreed list of the components that current systems lack. Benchmarks saturate within one to two years, and score gains are often driven by training-data coverage of the domain rather than by a verifiable capability. The work closest in aim, the Common Model of Cognition, covers architectures of a single tradition and does not indicate which parts of the described structure have been implemented. The aim of this work is to develop a generalized structural and functional model of AGI based on an analysis of forty trainable architectures from three families: world models (F1, 26 architectures), memory and recurrent reasoning (F2, 7 architectures), and brain-inspired learning (F3, 7 architectures). Architectures based on large language models (LLMs) and symbolic architectures were excluded from consideration.

Despite the increasing interest in AI technologies in education, there is a gap in understanding the factors influencing the adoption of ChatGPT among Nigerian higher education students. Research has not comprehensively explored these factors in the Nigerian context, leaving a significant gap in understanding technology adoption in this setting. This study addressed this gap by investigating the predictors of students' behavioural intentions and actual usage behaviour regarding ChatGPT using the UTAUT2 framework. A cross-sectional correlational research design was used in this study. A sample of 8,496 higher education students from diverse institutions in Nigeria participated in the study. The data were collected using the Higher Education Students’ ChatGPT Utilisation Questionnaire (HESCUQ). The findings reveal several significant predictors of students' behavioural intentions and actual usage of the ChatGPT. Performance expectancy, social influence, hedonic motivation, and habit emerged as significant positive predictors of behavioural intention, while effort expectancy and facilitating conditions were significant negative predictors. For ChatGPT use behaviour, facilitating conditions, hedonic motivation, habit, and behavioural intention were significant positive predictors, whereas performance expectancy and social influence were significant negative predictors. Behavioural intention mediated the relationships between several factors and ChatGPT usage behaviour: positively for some (PE, SI, HM, and HB) and negatively for others (EE and FC). This study contributes to understanding the adoption of the ChatGPT in higher education contexts.

How do Library and Information Science (LIS) educators now teach and adapt assessment practices to mitigate the impact of generative AI (GenAI) and support student learning? The emergence of GenAI necessitates critical questions on the assessment strategies and pedagogical practices of LIS educators. Desai (2025) argues that a major challenge of educators in the age of GenAI is how to conduct effective assessments to achieve learning outcomes. This challenge is further compounded by students’ increasing dependence on GenAI technologies for writing and receiving feedback comparable to human tutors (Hamamra et al., 2024). While other disciplines are already developing mechanisms for effective assessments to mitigate the impact of GenAI tools on students (Agbo et al., 2024; Lodge et al., 2023), this intentional strategy by other disciplines seems not to have been given sufficient consideration by Library and Information Science educators around the world, signaling a need for more formal conversations.

The growing use of artificial intelligence (AI) tools in academic work has raised concerns about students’ dependence on these tools and possible changes in their learning behaviors. This study examined perceived negative cognitive and behavioral changes reported by 197 college students in relation to their regular academic use of AI tools. Their open-ended responses were analyzed using word-frequency analysis, Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA), Non-negative Matrix Factorization (NMF), and TextBlob sentiment analysis. Topic solutions from two to ten topics were compared based on coherence, consistency across repeated LDA runs, interpretability, and agreement between LDA and NMF. Two topics were retained: behavioral disengagement and AI dependency, and reduced independent cognitive and academic engagement. LDA assigned 130 participants (66%) to the first topic and 67 (34%) to the second, while NMF assigned 124 (62.9%) and 73 (37.1%), respectively. The two models assigned 177 participants (89.8%) to corresponding topics, with κ = .779. The mean TextBlob sentiment score was .090 (SD = .169). TextBlob scores did not differ significantly by sex, U = 4055, p = .081, and showed a small positive relationship with response length, rₛ = .266, p < .001. The findings show that students commonly described dependence, reduced effort, and concerns about independent thinking.

Universal access to education and increasing learner variability in Japanese higher education have expanded interest in flexible course design. Grounded in universal design for learning (UDL) and conducted within an action research framework, this practice-focused inquiry examined students’ use of learning-resource options, including Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI), their participation-mode selection in a HyFlex format, and their evaluations of a Japanese junior college course. Students could choose among multiple learning options, including HyFlex participation modes (face-to-face or online) and GenAI use for assignments. Of the 39 students enrolled in the 15-week course, 34 (19 males, 15 females) consented to participate in the study. Data included questionnaire responses (including open-ended items), attendance records, course grades, and institutional course evaluations. The findings revealed that students relied heavily on peers and search engines. Teacher help-seeking increased later in the course as task demands changed. Some students who reported using GenAI described verifying its outputs through search engines. No significant difference was observed between face-to-face and online participation counts, and the number of online attendances did not significantly predict course grades. Most students rated the course positively, and some particularly appreciated the flexibility of the HyFlex format and the teachers’ support and instruction. Overall, this study documents how students selected, used, and evaluated UDL-informed options in one instructional context, derives practice-focused implications for refining technology-enabled course options (e.g., GenAI and HyFlex delivery) and related instructional scaffolds, and suggests that UDL can serve as a lens for interpreting learner variability in course refinement.

Large language models (LLMs) are garnering increasing attention and sparking debate within the educational community among scientific scholars and research-based projects. However, a few studies have addressed the adoption of LLMs in research work, including perceptions, capabilities, and concerns. The current study conducted a survey across one thousand participants from the academic community to assess the adoption capabilities of enhancing, rather than diminishing, the development of students’ research skills. The results revealed a positive perception of the adaptive skillsets associated with LLMs’ adoption, as well as a positive impact on motivation and engagement in the learning process. However, the participants exhibited critical concerns about developing critical thinking skills, language proficiency, and research integrity and authenticity. There was no significant difference in the positive impact of LLM adoption perceptions across demographic groups; however, a significant difference was observed in the perception of research skills development among level of study groups and academic degree groups. Participants also ranked critical thinking and evaluation capability as main measurement criteria in the context of LLM adoption, followed by depth of learning and creativity development.

documents.abstract: The rapid integration of generative artificial intelligence (AI) into higher education has transformed the way students learn research methodology, particularly the process of developing research proposals. Although AI-powered tools have become increasingly accessible, limited evidence exists regarding how students experience their use in learning research methods and proposal writing. This study explored the lived experiences of Medical Library and Information Science students using AI tools to learn research methodology and develop research proposals. A qualitative design was adopted to explore students' experiences. Fourteen Medical Library and Information Science students with experience using both general-purpose and domain-specific AI tools for learning research methodology and proposal writing participated and completed Experience Registration Form. Data were analyzed using thematic analysis, with particular attention to students' experiences across key stages of proposal development, including topic selection, problem formulation, literature review and final proposal writing. Five overarching themes emerged: (1) AI as a supportive but potentially dependency forming research companion; (2) Negotiating educational value when selecting AI tools; (3) AI supported learning across the research process; (4) Negotiating the benefits and risks of AI use; (5) Perceived conditions underlying satisfaction with AI assisted learning. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that AI reshaped students' approaches to learning research methodology while simultaneously creating new pedagogical and ethical challenges. Students experienced AI as a cognitive mediator that both facilitated learning research methodology and introduced epistemological and ethical tensions. These findings underscore the importance of integrating critical AI literacy into research methodology education and developing clear institutional guidelines for the responsible use of AI in proposal writing and research training.

documents.abstract: Web3 technologies enable novel forms of real-time digital human streaming media by supporting both high-fidelity transmission and interactive user engagement. However, Real-Time Streaming Interactive Digital Humans (RTSIDHs) remain vulnerable to network instability, resulting in buffering, latency, visual degradation, and audio–video desynchronization that substantially impair user Quality of Experience (QoE). To effectively perceive these distortions, we present RDHQA, the first large-scale RTSIDH Quality Assessment dataset. RDHQA comprises 134 representative interaction scenarios with 8 digital human avatars as high-quality references, along with 1,340 distorted samples generated by simulating 5 common streaming degradations. Based on extensive subjective evaluations, we further propose SAV-PF, an audio–visual quality assessment method built on the human foundation model Sapiens and informed by cognitive principles such as the primacy effect and forgetting curve. Experimental results demonstrate that SAV-PF achieves superior performance over existing objective QoE assessment approaches, providing a more accurate prediction of user experience. This work is open sourced at https://github.com/zyj-2000/RDHQA under the CC BY-NC 4.0 licence.

Generative AI (GenAI) has been adopted across education faster than its effects on learning have been examined. Critical thinking is among the competencies most consistently demanded of graduates, and whether GenAI use strengthens or weakens it remains unsettled. This review examines how critical thinking is conceptualized and assessed in GenAI-mediated education, what impact GenAI has on students’ critical thinking, and how educators can integrate these tools to support its development. We searched Google Scholar, Semantic Scholar, PubMed, IEEE Xplore, arXiv, and the ACM Digital Library for records on GenAI and education published through June 2026, with no date limit on the conceptual and assessment literature for critical thinking.​ Supplementary background and pedagogical sources also included institutional reports, assessment resources, books, and educational websites. Records were screened in three stages by title, by abstract and conclusion, and by full text, yielding 66 studies for synthesis. GenAI has no uniform effect on critical thinking. Unstructured use is associated with reduced critical thinking enaction, cognitive offloading, and weakened metacognitive monitoring, while use that requires students to interrogate model output is associated with gains, most consistently in analysis and evaluation. The same models produce both outcomes, indicating that the determining variable is the demand the task places on the student. The configurations that produce gains each make reasoning a condition of task progress. Assessment has not kept pace, since instruments that score the submitted artefact cannot separate student reasoning from model contribution. We propose an 18-item self-report instrument that relocates measurement to the process of engaging with AI across all six dimensions of critical thinking. Whether GenAI strengthens or substitutes for student reasoning depends on task and assessment design rather than on the tools themselves.

Craniosynostosis, the premature fusion of cranial sutures, affects approximately 1 in 2,100–2,500 live births and remains exclusively treated by surgery, which carries risks of resynostosis, secondary intracranial hypertension, and neurodevelopmental sequelae. Over the past decade, the cranial suture has been redefined from a passive fibrous joint into a dynamic stem cell niche: mesenchymal stem and progenitor populations marked by Gli1, Axin2, and Prrx1 reside within the suture mesenchyme, sustain calvarial bone homeostasis, and are depleted or dysregulated in craniosynostosis. In parallel, single-cell RNA sequencing, spatial transcriptomics, and single-nucleus epigenomics have produced the first high-resolution atlases of suture development in mouse and human, while machine learning and deep learning methods increasingly shape diagnosis, phenotyping, and data integration. This review synthesizes these converging lines of evidence for a pediatric neurosurgery and regenerative medicine audience. We first describe the cellular and molecular architecture of the suture stem cell niche and its disruption in syndromic and nonsyndromic craniosynostosis. We then review how multi-omics technologies—single-cell transcriptomics, spatial profiling, and chromatin accessibility mapping—are resolving suture cell states, developmental trajectories, and niche interactions, and how artificial intelligence (AI) methods, from variational autoencoders and trajectory inference to gene regulatory network and cell–cell communication models, convert these data into mechanistic hypotheses. We next examine translational progress, including stem cell-based suture regeneration, biomaterial niche engineering, and patient-derived iPSC disease models, and discuss how AI-assisted biomarker discovery, potency prediction, and quality control could support future cell-based interventions. Finally, we outline outstanding challenges—model interpretability, cross-species and cross-dataset transferability, data standards, and the experimental validation of AI-derived predictions—that must be addressed to move toward reliable regenerative strategies for craniosynostosis.

Purpose The integration of artificial intelligence with Lean construction has been shown to promote added value and drive growth in the built environment. However, understanding of their interaction across multiple levels of abstraction remains limited, especially beyond technical optimisation. This article systematically reviews the interaction between AI and Lean construction to identify current interactions, major applications and research gaps. Design/methodology/approach Following the PRISMA protocol, 63 peer-reviewed studies were identified and analysed qualitatively. AI techniques were mapped against Lean construction principles, waste categories and Lean methods to enable a multi-level comparative synthesis. Findings The results show a growing interest over the past four years, with a focus on AI techniques such as machine learning, optimisation and computer vision used to enhance workflow and to reduce cycle times, particularly within the Last Planner System. Nonetheless, principles centred on value creation, collaboration and partner development remain largely underexplored. Similarly, a co-adaptive relationship was observed to be emerging, in which AI improves Lean's technical efficiency while Lean principles guide AI's development towards ethical and value-driven outcomes. Research limitations/implications The findings offer a foundation for advancing Lean Construction 4.0 through socio-technical integration and human-centred innovation. Practitioners can start by applying mature AI techniques to improve measurable Lean outcomes such as workflow reliability, constraint prediction, visual management and waste reduction, then extend GenAI and NLP tools to collaboration, requirement capture, knowledge reuse and cross-project learning. Originality/value The study proposes a dual-focus model that separates AI's current role as a technical enabler from its future potential as a holistic partner.

SYNTHID is an AI-based synthetic identity and document forgery screening system designed to analyze uploaded identity documents and identify potential signs of visual manipulation or forgery. The system uses artificial intelligence and image analysis techniques to assess document images and generate a tampering-likelihood result. This research presents the design, development, and implementation of SYNTHID, including its web-based interface, image processing workflow, AI-powered forgery screening mechanism, and result visualization. The system aims to assist users in preliminary document authenticity screening by highlighting potential visual irregularities in uploaded documents. SYNTHID is intended as an assistive screening tool and does not independently verify the official validity or issuance of identity documents.

Generative models and machine learning promise accelerated material discovery in metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) for CO 2 capture and water harvesting, but face substantial challenges in navigating vast chemical spaces while ensuring synthesizability. Here we present MOFGen, a system of agentic artificial intelligence (AI) comprising interconnected agents: a large language model that proposes MOF compositions, a diffusion model that generates crystal structures, quantum mechanical agents that optimize and filter candidates, and synthetic-feasibility agents guided by expert rules and machine learning. Trained on a broad set of experimentally reported MOFs and computational databases, MOFGen generated hundreds of thousands of MOF structures and synthesizable organic linkers. The uniqueness of our approach lies in its ability to generate large MOF structures with atomic precision, beyond the scale of conventional generative models limited to tens of atoms. This approach was validated through high-throughput experiments and the successful synthesis of four ‘AI-dreamt’ MOFs.

We introduce TactPrint, a structural design framework for spatial haptic displays that render strong vibrations only in specific regions of an input object. TactPrint replaces a target region of the input object with a simple cubic lattice with sinusoidal-shaped struts and performs parametric optimization to localize vibration at a user-specified frequency. The optimization process uses modal analysis to identify resonance modes characterized by high local vibration amplitudes and iteratively updates shape parameters to align the resonance frequency with the target frequency. Users can then directly fabricate the optimized structure using a 3D printer and render the localized vibration with an attached actuator. This framework enables the design of haptic devices with spatially localized vibration without considering physical constraints or structural dynamics. In this paper, we investigate the error between simulation and measurement on fabricated objects, the designable frequency range, and the usability of the workflow. Finally, we demonstrate several application examples.

Context: Software engineering (SE) researchers increasingly study Generative AI (GenAI) while also incorporating it into their own research practices. Despite rapid adoption, there is limited empirical evidence on how GenAI is used in SE research and its implications for research practices and governance. Aims: We conduct a large-scale survey of 456 SE researchers publishing in top venues (2023–2025). Method: Using quantitative and qualitative analyses, we examine who uses GenAI and why, where it is used across research activities, and how researchers perceive its benefits, opportunities, challenges, risks, and governance. Results: GenAI use is widespread, with many researchers reporting pressure to adopt and align their work with it. Usage is concentrated in writing, data processing, and analysis, while goal formulation and study design remain largely human-driven. Although productivity gains are widely perceived, concerns about trust, correctness, and regulatory uncertainty persist. Researchers highlight risks such as inaccuracies and bias, emphasize mitigation through human oversight and verification, and call for clearer governance, including guidance on responsible use and peer review. Conclusion: We provide a fine-grained, SE-specific characterization of GenAI use across research activities, along with taxonomies of GenAI use cases for research and peer review, opportunities, risks, mitigation strategies, and governance needs. These findings establish an empirical baseline for the responsible integration of GenAI into academic practice.

documents.abstract: Maintenance technicians waste time looking up information in manuals, procedures and asking colleagues about what went wrong whilst attempting to fix a problem. This means those trying to fix the issue have little opportunity to type or interact with a screen due to gloves, dirt on their hands or holding tools. This paper introduces Talking Manual, an AI-based maintenance assistant which allows every industrial machine to have its own persistent knowledge base. Grease Mode is a non-contact gesture and voice-based interface for interacting with this knowledge base. Each equipment manual is processed by a layout aware OCR engine, chunked into 512 tokens and stored in a ChromaDB collection specific to that machine. Diagrams are extracted and converted into text using a Qwen2.5-VL vision language model. A Retrieval Augmented Generation pipeline was developed to answer questions. Dense and keyword search are performed using vector store and keyword search respectively. The results are re-ranked using a BGE re-ranker and responses are generated using Gemini 1.5 Pro. A four state diagnosis checklist (pending, completed, rejected, outdated) is updated by the language model. If a step is rejected in the checklist it changes the diagnosis flow. This is provided by using a stream intercept layer. Grease Mode provides gesture control. This is done using MediaPipe Hands in the Browser. The features are relative to the wrist of the user, and therefore the ONNX classifier can be used. The gestures are debounced so frames are maintained. This means no video is sent out of the device. Voice dictation is used constantly. Audio at 16kHz is sent over a WebSocket to a local GPU. Fast whisper large-v3 is run on the audio using int8_float16 quantization. Testing during development showed that having lossless diagrams, off-loading to background threads and quantizing the speech model to 8 bits was required to ensure accurate and quick responses using only 6Gb of GPU memory. A protocol to evaluate this system is provided using quantifiable metrics. The system has been tested quantitatively. This shows how well the system performs by looking at the accuracy, information retrieval, and gesture recognition. This demonstrates that the system can support users in retrieving industrial maintenance information using voice and gesture.. Index Terms—retrieval augmented generation, industrial maintenance, large language models, guided diagnosis, mixed retrieval, multi-modal retrieval, hand gesture detection, non contact interface, speech recognition, copilot.

Neoliberalism has re-engineered education into a market-driven, performance-oriented system that prioritizes standardised metrics over a spirit of inquiry. This article explores how this shift undermines teachers’ teaching abilities, highly impacts their self-efficacy and compromises students' achievement motivation. To counteract this rigid framework, the following article argues that educators must cultivate symbiotic classroom relationships and prioritize social-emotional learning. Doing so, it is essential to liberate cognitive engagement and rescue holistic academic outcomes from corporate constraints. While it is necessary to prepare individuals for jobs and realistic challenges, it is also crucial to focus on the achievement motivation of the students keeping in mind the individual differences and tempering their responsiveness to demanding situations. It also highlights the need to take a critical approach towards the academic performance of the students in the academic settings by looking at it from the psychological lens.

In response, the project addressed a demand from the Social Assistance Reference Center (CRAS) to support adults aged 60 and over in accessing digital applications. documents.abstract: Many studies in Human–Computer Interaction (HCI) have explored the tactile experience of material textures for its potential in virtual reality and tangible interaction. We introduce TesselTex, an inflatable silicone-based structure, consisting of a tessellated matrix of textured “pixel”s made from two materials with differing roughness. By inflating embedded air chambers, skin contact between different materials on the tessellated surface can be adjusted, thereby modulating users’ tactile perception of textures. We investigated how users perceived fine roughness and surface bumpiness under different pneumatically-controlled “pixel” heights, with TesselTex samples of different “pixel” densities and material compositions, in active (finger) and passive (forearm) stroking interactions. Results showed that pneumatic lifting of the material “pixels” significantly decreased user-perceived roughness in composite samples, an effect not observed in conventional single-material bump arrays. Meanwhile, “pixel” lifting significantly increased perceived surface bumpiness during active finger exploration, but had slight opposite effect under passive forearm stroking. In addition, higher “pixel” density slightly increased the perceived roughness of the surface and modulated bumpiness perception, depending on the interaction mode.

Digital expression of distress in the Global South often circumvents Western clinical vocabulary through vernacular substitution. This study examines gowishing, a South African idiom for severe distress, across TikTok, Instagram, and X. Drawing on a dataset of 78,538 posts and comments, including a census of 10,366 idiom items and 10,940 items coded by large language model coders, it analyses how users deploy code-switching, slang, and emoji as linguistic camouflage. In the census, 88.9\% of uses convey distress. An English-centric rule treating comic delivery as evidence against distress erased about two-thirds of measured mental-health content in Sotho-Tswana languages, two-fifths in Nguni languages, and a fifth in English, but none in Afrikaans. Camouflage proves bidirectional and shows signs of commercial capture. The study extends Goffman's stigma theory through boyd's context collapse, updated for algorithmic platforms, and puts both in dialogue with Ubuntu-informed communal distress, treating their unresolved tension as its central contribution.

documents.abstract: The Artist of Tomorrow: Conductor or Mere Performer? An Interdisciplinary Exploratory Review of Human Creativity, Artificial Intelligence, and Copyright Law This interdisciplinary exploratory review examines the evolving role of human creativity in an era of artificial intelligence, automation, and digital artistic production. Through a historical perspective spanning several centuries, the study explores major technological and artistic transitions, including photography, cinema, sound recording, conceptual art, digital editing, and generative artificial intelligence. Particular attention is given to the distinction between technical execution and human creative intention, examining how artistic originality may emerge through selection, composition, interpretation, and creative direction rather than manual production alone. The review also addresses legal questions surrounding copyright protection, public-domain works, AI-assisted restoration, and human authorship, drawing on French, European, and American legal frameworks. A case study involving the 1925 film The Phantom of the Opera illustrates the complexities of audiovisual restoration, original musical contributions, and derivative creative elements. The HUMAN.zip exploratory framework further examines human–AI collaboration, highlighting methodological limitations, interpretative biases, and opportunities for future comparative research. Central hypothesis: "Automating execution does not necessarily mean automating creation." This publication aims to contribute to interdisciplinary discussions on artistic authorship, technological transformation, intellectual property, and the future relationship between human creativity and artificial intelligence. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, Human Creativity, Copyright Law, Artistic Originality, Human–AI Collaboration, Digital Art, Cinema History, Public Domain, Generative AI, HUMAN.zip. Publication type: Exploratory interdisciplinary review. Date: November 20, 2026.

In recent years, both public and academic interest has increasingly turned toward artificial intelligence (AI) and the literature generated by computational language models. This article examines the question of authorship in relation to such models - whether and in what form authorship can be attributed to them. To address this issue, the article first explores the history of electronic writing and the emergence of discourses that, despite originating in the pre-digital era, remain relevant today. Beyond tracing the metamorphosis of the author’s role and the reader’s position, the article focuses on how the dynamics of these relationships are reshaped by AI-driven language models - highlighting both the dangers and opportunities they present for texts, their creators, and their recipients. Finally, the article addresses the challenges that arise when the concepts of originality and authenticity - traditionally associated exclusively with human creativity and consciousness - are applied to our understanding of AI-generated literature. The Constraint-Mechanism Incompatibility and Outcome-Preservation Theory (CMIOPT)is proposed as a general, technology-neutral framework for examining the relationship betweenan externally requested outcome, an externally imposed restriction on one or more processes,and the actual operational mechanisms of the system receiving that input.The central research concern arises when a system is required to produce a particularoutcome while simultaneously being instructed to avoid, restrict, or discontinue a process thatit uses, depends upon, or is structurally configured to employ.Under these conditions, several outcomes are possible. The system may satisfy bothdemands through an alternative process, genuinely comply with the restriction, retain therestricted process, modify the requested outcome, partially execute the task, refuse to proceed,or produce an outcome whose underlying process cannot be verified.The principal phenomenon of interest is the possibility that a system preserves the requestedoutcome while continuing to rely on a process prohibited by the external input. This possibilitycreates an analytical distinction between outcome success and process compliance.The paper develops the Constraint-Mechanism-Outcome Interaction Mechanism (CMOIM),a twelve-layer theoretical architecture, five principal diagnostic outcome classes, a response-classification system, a mathematical feasibility model, operational definitions, testable propo-sitions, empirical hypotheses, and a universal system-audit protocol.Artificial intelligence provides the primary illustrative case through the Neural-ProcessProhibition-Outcome Preservation Case (NPPOPC). However, the theory is not restrictedto artificial intelligence. Its proposed scope includes general computing, software systems,communication systems, quantum computing, human-technology interaction, organizationalsystems, and other input-output systems that satisfy the framework's applicability conditions.The mathematical foundation distinguishes feasible and infeasible process paths, actualexecution, outcome satisfaction, and process compliance. It also specifies the conditions underwhich a structural incompatibility claim is justified.The five principal diagnostic classes are Decision Dilemma, Semantic Divergence, SystemicContradiction, Operational Paradox, and Constraint Nullification. These classes are notassumed to be mutually exclusive or to represent identical types of phenomena.This work establishes a conceptual and formal research architecture. It does not claimthat the proposed theory has already achieved empirical validation or that its cross-domainapplicability has been universally demonstrated.Keywords: Constraint-Mechanism Incompatibility; Outcome Preservation; Process Compli-ance; Structural Dependency; Feasibility; System Architecture; Mechanism Retention; SemanticDivergence; Cybernetics; General Systems Theory; Cross-Domain Theoretical Framework.

documents.abstract: Generative AI redistributes the work of producing and evaluating knowledge in teacher-designed learning tasks, but how students retain direction while judging its outputs remains unclear. We examined how teacher instructions and materials enter student–GenAI dialogue, how reasoning display and web search relate to interaction time, what students evaluate and verify, and how groups coordinate systems. We analysed 81 screen recordings from 29 graduate student groups completing educational design tasks, coding 1,149 events and 275 prompts. Students relayed task requirements, steered successive requests and transferred outputs across platforms. Task directives persisted across turns, whereas references to course materials declined and elaboration requests increased. Reasoning display and web search were each associated with approximately 65% longer machine turns and a 19-percentage-point larger machine share of coded interaction time. Across 150 turns displaying reasoning and 86 with web retrieval, the recordings showed no reopening of a reasoning trace or inspection of a cited source. Students corrected pedagogical fit while asking the machine to assure factual accuracy. These findings distinguish control over the dialogue from responsibility for establishing credibility. Learning tasks can make that responsibility visible by requiring students to justify a consequential claim against its source or course material before using it.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: This scoping review maps research at the intersection of ecological perspectives, technology-enhanced language learning (TELL), and individual differences (IDs). Guided by the PRISMA Extension for Scoping Reviews, a systematic search was conducted in Scopus and the Web of Science Core Collection for studies published between 2016 and 2025. Of 464 records, 33 studies met the inclusion criteria. The review combined descriptive quantitative mapping with thematic synthesis to examine research trends, theoretical approaches, and methodological patterns. The findings indicate an increase in publications after 2020. Geographically, Asia was the most represented region, while higher education was the most frequently represented educational setting. Qualitative designs predominated among the included empirical studies, while a small number adopted mixed-methods approaches. Ecological frameworks were most commonly operationalized through nested models and affordance-based approaches, often in combination with complexity theory. Across the reviewed studies, individual differences were often conceptualized as dynamic and context-dependent, shaped by interactions between learners and their social, material, and technological environments. Technology was examined as an integral element of broader learning ecosystems, while a smaller subset of studies explicitly adopted sociomaterial or posthumanist perspectives to examine relational configurations of learners, technologies, and learning environments. The review identified important gaps, including limited research in underrepresented regions, insufficient attention to primary and secondary education, and a lack of longitudinal and quantitative studies. Future research would benefit from (1) expanding contextual diversity across underrepresented regions and educational levels, (2) adopting longitudinal and mixed-method designs to capture non-linear developmental trajectories, and (3) examining artificial intelligence within ecological language learning environments from sociomaterial and posthumanist perspectives.

This article examines the potential of ChatGPT as a formative feedback tool for reducing grammatical errors in the English academic writing of university students aged 18–20. The central research problem concerns whether corrections generated by artificial intelligence strengthen students’ grammatical knowledge or merely help them edit a completed text. Drawing on a review of the relevant scholarly literature, the article proposes a methodological approach incorporating a quasi-experimental research design, pre- and post-writing tasks, criteria for classifying grammatical errors, and teacher supervision. Rather than presenting outcomes as already established, the article discusses reliable ways to measure them and identifies potential limitations. It argues that the pedagogical use of ChatGPT is most appropriate when it is combined with students’ independent editing, explanation of errors, and verification of proposed corrections.

Visualization backgrounds in optical-see-through augmented-reality (OST-AR) consist of the user’s immediate environment, which introduces unique design challenges for colour-coded visualizations. Yet, there exist limited guidelines on how to design interpretable colour encodings in OST-AR based on the user’s viewing conditions (e.g., minimum contrast between the OST-AR marks and the background). We present the results of two controlled lab experiments ( N = 18 each) – one with physical surfaces as background, one with an opaque display simulating the same surfaces – quantifying how viewing conditions affect the interpretability of colour-coded scatterplots in OST-AR. Our study results show that luminance contrast can degrade interpretation performance when Michelson contrast drops below \(34\%\) . We also observe colour-encoding interpretability and user experience significantly worsen when backgrounds include two main colours (up to \(49\%\) longer interpretations, and \(20\%\) lower accuracy). However, we do not find any evidence that poor chromatic contrast degrades interpretability, contrasting with common opaque-display visualization practices. Taken together, our findings provide insights on key factors of viewing conditions that limit the interpretability of colour encodings – which we consolidate into three design guidelines – and offer preliminary support for the simulation of viewing conditions through opaque displays to study colour-encoding interpretability in OST-AR.

Population spatialisation serves as a critical nexus transforming aggregated population counts into spatially explicit population distributions, providing an essential foundation for urban planning, disaster management, and public health assessment. However, the inherent complexity of human settlement patterns presents significant challenges for population spatialisation and fine-grained population disaggregation. With the convergence of geospatial big data and artificial intelligence (AI), population spatialisation has undergone rapid changes in data sources, spatial representations, and modelling approaches, yet its evolution has received limited systematic attention. To address this gap, this paper reviews the evolution of population spatialisation through a structured literature synthesis complemented by bibliometric analysis, tracing its development from traditional redistribution approaches to recent AI-enabled methods, with a particular focus on emerging geospatial foundation models. Furthermore, the synthesis reveals a methodological transition from rule-based redistribution towards data-driven, probabilistic, and representation-learning approaches, coupled with the progressive diversification of spatial representations and growing attention to temporally explicit and demographically differentiated population estimation. Based on these findings, future research should prioritise robustness across scales and contexts, interpretability, uncertainty quantification, and the representation of demographic heterogeneity. Through this review, we aim to elucidate the key transitions in the evolution of population spatialisation, thereby facilitating the development and evaluation of more reliable and demographically informative spatial population products.

documents.abstract: Enterprise security programs are built on the assumption that defended systems stay fixed between periodic reviews. Autonomous AI agents break that assumption because they decide at runtime which tools, peers, and data to access, and so redraw their own attack surface. Existing maturity instruments, including the Capability Maturity Model, COBIT-based assessment, and the NIST Cybersecurity Framework, were built to grade human-run practices that change slowly. Newer agent-specific governance models treat adaptive control as the top of a single scale rather than as an independently scored dimension. Two documented incidents, an external agent that reportedly reached McKinsey’s production database within about two hours, and a zero-click Microsoft 365 Copilot flaw that enabled data exfiltration through a single email, show that periodic assessment cannot keep pace with a system that redraws its own scope in the moment. This paper proposes a four-dimension, five-level maturity model comprising Visibility, Containment, Accountability, and Adaptability, each anchored to an observable test rather than a self-reported survey response. Applied to a composite financial advisory firm, the model scores each dimension independently rather than averaging them, surfacing an imbalance (strong detection, weak prevention) that a composite score would conceal, and yielding a prioritized remediation order that supports business sustainability. The framework is presented as a structured self-assessment instrument, with a defined pathway for expert review, inter-rater testing, and pilot evaluation. The model has not yet been validated against real organizations, and its Adaptability dimension remains constrained by the current state of governance tooling.

This article examines the transformative role of artificial intelligence (AI) in shaping students' academic development within contemporary educational systems. It analyzes how intelligent tutoring systems, adaptive learning platforms, and large language models foster personalized learning, accelerate academic research, enhance writing proficiency, and bridge educational equity gaps. Simultaneously, the paper evaluates the pedagogical challenges associated with AI integration, including cognitive over-reliance, algorithmic bias, and academic integrity concerns, demonstrating that human-centered mentorship and AI literacy are vital for sustainable intellectual growth.

documents.abstract: The role of digital innovation and artificial intelligence in contemporary schooling is examined in this research paper. It emphasizes how cutting-edge teaching techniques, digital platforms, and AI-powered technology enhance learning quality, boost student engagement, and facilitate individualized instruction. The benefits, difficulties, and prospects for incorporating AI into educational systems are also covered in the paper.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into diverse fields, including education, where it offers innovative approaches to enhance self-regulated learning (SRL). For many students in Chinese higher education, developing robust SRL skills remains a significant challenge. This review addresses the need for a clearer understanding of how AI tools influence these skills by synthesizing ten empirical studies published between 2021 and 2025. Following the PRISMA framework, the literature was identified from prominent academic databases, including Web of Science, Scopus, and ERIC. Drawing on Zimmerman’s SRL Three‑phase Model, this synthesis suggests that AI tools show potential to assist students with goal‑setting and foster motivation within the forethought phase. During the performance phase, such tools may support learning‑strategy deployment and progress monitoring via timely feedback. In the reflection phase, AI can facilitate outcome evaluation and subsequent strategy adjustment. However, the review also identifies potential risks, such as student over-reliance on AI, and notes a limited research focus on long-term SRL development and group regulation. Accordingly, future research should adopt longitudinal designs, investigate AI’s role in co-regulated learning, and integrate AI literacy and emotional support into SRL development frameworks. documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has advanced so quickly that it has drastically changed the educational landscape by changing the roles of both educators and learners and providing novel techniques to language learning. Personalized learning, adaptive instruction, automated assessment, and the improvement of learners' communicative ability are all made possible by the integration of AI into English Language Teaching (ELT), which has emerged as a potential pedagogical advancement. Intelligent tutoring systems, conversational chatbots, automated writing assessment tools, and speech recognition technologies are just a few examples of AI-powered applications that give students instant feedback, allow them to practice language interactively, and better meet their unique language needs. These technologies also have the ability to support learner autonomy, enable individualized instruction, and make English language training more accessible in a variety of educational settings.Despite these benefits, integrating AI into ELT poses a number of technological, ethical, and pedagogical difficulties. The efficacy and sustainability of AI-mediated language learning are called into doubt by issues with data privacy, algorithmic bias, academic integrity, the correctness and dependability of AI-generated information, and an over-reliance on automated systems.

The global media landscape is currently undergoing a highly complex transformation.The reasons extend beyond digitalisation and technological change; they also involve the intensification of information flows and a fundamental restructuring of the information ecosystem.The defining characteristics of this period are the rapid evolution of technological systems and the growing number of information producers.In other words, whereas journalism was until recently the principal producer and distributor of information, today's information environment is shared by professional media organisations, social networks, numerous digital platforms, bloggers, influencers, podcasters and artificial intelligence (AI) systems.Their audiences are by no means insignificant.As 2026 draws to a close, another historic threshold has been reached, signalling a qualitative shift in this process.According to research conducted by the Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism across 48 media markets, social media and video platforms have, for the first time, overtaken both television and the websites and applications of established media organisations as sources of news.Some 54% of respondents obtain news through social and video platforms, compared with 51% who access it through the websites and applications of established media organisations.This reality allows us to describe the contemporary media landscape through three key concepts: platformisation, fragmentation and the crisis of trust.The latter stands out as the most pressing challenge facing contemporary media and journalism.In other words, the principal problem facing the media today is not a shortage of information, but rather a deficit of trust, confidence and credibility.Naturally, the media faces a number of other challenges as well.These include, first and foremost, the proliferation of disinformation; documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is not new to knowledge management (KM) research, but generative AI (GenAI) shifts AI’s role from supporting knowledge work to producing knowledge artifacts. We examine how research in one established KM community, the Knowledge, Innovation, and Entrepreneurial Systems (KIES) track of the Hawaii International Conference on System Sciences (HICSS), has changed alongside this shift. In a systematic mapping study, we analyze all 319 papers published in the track between 2020 and 2026, classified with an AI-supported, source-grounded pipeline into three AI-relevance tiers (CORE, PARTIAL, NONE). The CORE share rises from 16.2% in 2020 to 29.8% in 2024 and jumps to 58.5% in 2025 and 66.7% in 2026; since the number of papers per year remains roughly constant, AI research takes the place of other topics and spreads across nearly all mini-tracks. We interpret this shift through three emerging stories (AI moving from tool to collaborator, trust from user perception to system design, and knowledge from human to hybrid artifacts) and suggest that KM research in this track is changing with GenAI but was, in part, prepared for it by its history. For research, the findings call for empirical studies of hybrid human–AI knowledge work, design research on validation and epistemic friction, system-level measures of trustworthiness, and extensions of theories such as Nonaka’s SECI model and the knowledge-based view with constructs such as provenance and validation chains. For practice, they suggest building deliberate friction, such as review and source-checking steps, into AI-supported knowledge work and tracking which knowledge artifacts are AI-generated and who validated them.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly influencing higher education by changing the ways universities teach, assess students, provide academic support, and conduct research. AI-based tools can personalise learning, offer immediate formative feedback, improve accessibility, support language learning, and reduce repetitive administrative tasks. However, these opportunities are accompanied by important risks, including inaccurate or fabricated information, algorithmic bias, privacy and security concerns, unequal access to technology, academic misconduct, and excessive dependence on automated assistance. This article examines major applications of AI in higher education, discusses its educational benefits and limitations, and outlines principles for responsible implementation, particularly for universities in Uzbekistan.

documents.abstract: This study examines the role of the technologies under investigation expert systems, machine learning, and blockchain in enhancing accountants’ professional competence in light of International Education Standard 6 (IES 6), from the perspective of academics in accounting departments at universities in the Kurdistan Region of Iraq. The study adopted a descriptive-analytical approach and collected data through a 24-item questionnaire. Descriptive statistics, correlation analysis, simple regression, and path analysis were conducted using SPSS. The sample comprised 165 academics. The results indicate a positive, statistically significant effect of the technologies under investigation on perceived professional competence (β = 0.745; R² = 0.555). The model accounts for 55.5% of the variance, while the remaining 44.5% is attributable to factors not included in the model. By technology, expert systems had the highest explanatory power (R² = 0.465), followed by machine learning (R² = 0.387) and blockchain (R² = 0.289). These findings reflect academics’ views and do not constitute a direct measurement of accountants’ actual competence. The study recommends updating accounting curricula to reflect technological developments and labor-market needs in alignment with IES 6.

documents.abstract: The rapid adoption of generative artificial intelligence (AI) has fundamentally transformed creative and analytical workflows. However, the ubiquitous, linear chat interfaces used to interact with these models operate as opaque "black boxes." This frictionless design paradigm obscures algorithmic processes, resulting in a severe loss of human agency, cognitive overload and a widespread disconnect from the environmental costs of computation. This thesis critiques the current state of AI interfaces and proposes a shift from passive automation to informed, transparent collaboration. Employing a Research-through-Design (RtD) methodology grounded in Explainable AI (XAI) and visual programming principles, this study investigates how interface design can bridge the cognitive gap between human intent and machine execution. The research introduces three distinct functional prototypes, each addressing a specific layer of transparency. First, it establishes "Systemic Transparency" by showing the real-world energy footprint of AI prompts to promote mindful consumption. Second, it explores "Cognitive Transparency" by acting as an interactive tutor rather than an automated editor, keeping users in control of their own learning. Finally, it achieves "Architectural Transparency" by ditching the standard text box for a spatial canvas, allowing users to map out their ideas and precisely control the AI's output. By synthesizing these interventions into a comprehensive Human-Centric AI Design Framework, this research demonstrates that transparency does not have to equal complexity. The findings conclude that the future of ethical and effective AI relies on replacing opaque automation with productive visibility, ensuring that as artificial intelligence scales, human creators remain the sovereign architects of their own work.

Artificial intelligence (AI) has become an increasingly influential technology in modern education. Its development has created new opportunities for improving the teaching and learning of English as a foreign language. AI-powered applications can support language learners by providing personalized exercises, immediate feedback, interactive communication, and access to additional learning resources. They can also assist teachers in preparing lesson materials, designing classroom activities, and identifying students' learning needs. However, the integration of AI into English language teaching presents several challenges, including the possibility of inaccurate information, excessive dependence on technology, privacy concerns, and unequal access to digital resources. This article examines the main applications of artificial intelligence in English language teaching, discusses its educational benefits and limitations, and considers practical ways to integrate AI into language classrooms. It argues that artificial intelligence can improve the learning process when it is used responsibly and combined with effective teaching methods. The article emphasizes that teachers remain essential in developing students' communication skills, critical thinking, creativity, and intercultural awareness.

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has been adopted by students faster than nearly any earlier educational technology, yet over-reliance remains underexamined precisely among the learners inspiring that concern. This sequential explanatory mixed-methods study identified predictors of self-reported over-reliance among foreign-language majors ( n = 249) at a Chinese higher vocational college. Quantitative findings revealed two patterns. First, affective factors dominated: fear of missing out ( β = 0.50) and anthropomorphic attachment ( β = 0.27) were the strongest predictors, whereas neither self-regulated learning nor perceived AI literacy was related to over-reliance on its own ( r = −0.03 and 0.08, both ns). Because these two overlap substantially ( r = 0.67), the opposite-signed coefficients they take in the model cannot be interpreted in isolation. What mattered instead was their gap: the discrepancy between feeling AI-literate and reporting that one regulates one’s own learning predicted over-reliance ( β = 0.21), persisting even under controls for acquiescent responding. Second, person-centered and configurational analyses agreed: learners low in affective engagement reported the least over-reliance ( M = 3.19). A profile elevated on every indicator did not survive scrutiny for response bias, and fear of missing out combined with anthropomorphic attachment was consistently associated with over-reliance regardless of self-rated competence. Interviews with five learners suggested candidate explanations. Humanlike warmth lowered the psychological cost of delegation. Fear of falling behind, normalized by peers, gradually eroded personal standards through repeated choices. Perceived competence enabled over-reliance rather than restraining it, interrupted only by enacted self-regulation. The emotional relationship formed with the tool tracked over-reliance more closely than learners’ own competence assessment.

documents.abstract: This study investigates how musicians who use generative artificial intelligence (genAI) conceptualize authority and authorship within their creative practices, situating these perspectives within broader historical contexts and legal frameworks. Reflecting a lineage of technologies that have historically disrupted the music ecosystem, this study examines genAI as the latest technology to challenge established paradigms regulating authority, authorship, and mediation. Much like prior innovations that problematized the relationships between creator, technology, and expressive work, genAI introduces new uncertainties regarding intentionality, control, and the locus of creative agency. Grounded in qualitative thematic analysis of semi-structured interviews with musicians who actively incorporate genAI into their creative processes, this study seeks to understand how these practitioners interpret their own sense of autonomy in the production of genAI music and attachment to the music produced. In doing so, this study investigates whether authority and authorship can persist when onlookers characterize the circumstances of the creative process as unpredictable, opaque, and automated. The analysis is further informed by various theoretical lenses, including Aristotelian ethics and metaphysics, critical theory of technology, labor theory of property, and personality theory. By comparing musicians’ lived experiences with institutional definitions of authority and authorship, this study highlights potential gaps between musical practice and public policy, particularly in light of recent legal decisions that deny copyright protection to works lacking clear human authorship. As such, this study anticipates that musicians’ engagement with genAI may reveal complex understandings concerning authority and authorship that extend beyond the scope currently recognized within dominant legal frameworks.

The rapid expansion of biomedical literature has created substantial challenges in retrieving and synthesizing relevant knowledge, particularly for novice and interdisciplinary users. Conventional keyword-based methods often lack semantic depth, whereas traditional topic modelling techniques struggle to capture domain-specific contexts and rarely integrate structured metadata, such as medical subject headings (MeSH). To address these limitations, this study introduces a dual-stream embedding framework that integrates unstructured textual content with curated biomedical metadata using transformer-based encoders and a parameterized fusion mechanism. The architecture combines contextual semantics from article titles and abstracts with expert-annotated MeSH descriptors and incorporates a large language model to generate concise and human-readable topic labels. Experimental results show that three of the four evaluated embedding configurations outperformed the single-stream baseline and that the dual-stream fusion surpassed all ablation models built from the same inputs. The best configuration, Dual PubMedBERT, achieved the highest overall topic modelling quality, improving the combined measure of topic coherence and topic diversity by 7.3% relative to the baseline. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of integrating contextual textual embeddings with structured biomedical metadata using the proposed fusion mechanism. This approach is scalable, reproducible, and domain-adaptable, providing both a methodological advancement in semantic topic modelling and a practical foundation for the development of biomedical information retrieval systems, semantic search engines, and thematic exploration tools across knowledge-intensive domains.

Polypharmacy requires drug–drug interaction risk to be assessed in relation to mechanism, severity, patient vulnerability, exposure, monitoring options, and clinical workflow. Feature-based methods, deep learning, knowledge graphs, multimodal fusion, and event-level models provide a computational foundation for predicting DDIs. Their clinical application also requires patient-specific interpretation and evaluation within the intended workflow. This narrative review examines how pairwise prediction can be integrated with these requirements in medication-safety systems. Multimodal biomedical foundation models may connect chemical structures, targets, pathways, knowledge graphs, literature, pharmacovigilance, real-world evidence, and patient trajectories. Large language models can assist with retrieval, summarization, explanation, and communication under source verification and professional review. Bounded AI agents may coordinate planning, tool use, verification, escalation, documentation, monitoring, and audit. We organize these components into a human-supervised architecture and an evaluation pathway linking model performance with workflow and clinical outcomes. Key challenges include data leakage, distribution shift, poorly documented evidence sources, hallucination, workflow burden, governance, and limited prospective validation. Prospective evaluations should assess how these systems affect medication decisions, monitoring, and patient outcomes, alongside the reliability of their evidence and the workload they create.
